text: Man is a mystery: if you spend your entire life trying to puzzle it out, then do not say that you have wasted your time.
author: Fyodor Dostoevsky
source: Personal correspondence (1839), as quoted in Dostoevsky: His Life and Work (1971) by Konstantin Mochulski, as translated by Michael A. Minihan, p. 17

text: I am a child of this age, a child of unfaith and scepticism, and probably shall remain so to the end of my life. How dreadfully has it tormented me, this longing for faith, which is all the stronger for the proofs I have against it. And yet God gives me sometimes moments of perfect peace; in such moments I love and believe that I am loved; in such moments I have formulated my creed, wherein all is clear and holy to me. This creed is extremely simple: I believe that there is nothing lovelier, deeper, more sympathetic, more rational, more manly, and more perfect than the Saviour; I say to myself with jealous love that not only is there no one else like Him, but that there could be no one. I would even say more: If anyone could prove to me that Christ is outside the truth, and if the truth really did exclude Christ, I should prefer to stay with Christ and not with truth.
author: Fyodor Dostoevsky
source: Letter to Mme. N. D. Fonvisin (1854), as published in Letters of Fyodor Michailovitch Dostoevsky to his Family and Friends (1914), translated by Ethel Golburn Mayne, Letter XXI, p. 71

text: Neither a person nor a nation can exist without some higher idea. And there is only one higher idea on earth, and it is the idea of the immortality of the human soul, for all other "higher" ideas of life by which humans might live derive from that idea alone.
author: Fyodor Dostoevsky
source: A Writer's Diary , Vol. 1: 1873-1876 , ed. Kenneth Lantz (1994), p. 734

text: The wisest of all, in my opinion, is he who can, if only once a month, call himself a fool — a faculty unheard of nowadays. They have so muddled things up that there is no telling a fool from a wise man.
author: Fyodor Dostoevsky
source: "Bobok: From Somebody's Diary" (1873), as translated by Constance Garnett in Short Stories (New York: Books, Inc, 1900)

text: All writers who have sought to represent Absolute Beauty were unequal to the task, for it is an infinitely difficult one. There is in the world only one figure of absolute beauty: Christ. That infinitely lovely figure is, as a matter of course, an infinite marvel.
author: Fyodor Dostoevsky
source: Letter to his Niece Sofia Alexandrovna, Geneva, January 1, 1868. Ethel Golburn Mayne, Letters of Fyodor Michailovitch Dostoyevsky to His Family and Friends (1879), Dostoevsky's Letters XXXIX, p. 136

text: I am a sick man... I am a wicked man. An unattractive man.
author: Fyodor Dostoevsky
source: I am a sick man... I am a wicked man. An unattractive man.

text: I did not know how to become anything; neither spiteful nor kind, neither a rascal nor an honest man, neither a hero nor an insect. An intelligent man cannot become anything seriously, and it is only the fool who becomes anything.
author: Fyodor Dostoevsky

text: Once it's been proved to you that a single droplet of your own fat must be dearer to you than a hundred thousand of your fellow human beings and consequently that all so-called virtues and duties are nothing but ravings and prejudices, then accept that too, because there's nothing to be done.
author: Fyodor Dostoevsky

text: Civilization has made man, if not always more bloodthirsty, at least more viciously, more horribly bloodthirsty.
author: Fyodor Dostoevsky

text: The best definition of man is: a being that goes on two legs and is ungrateful.
author: Fyodor Dostoevsky
source: Part 1, Chapter 8 (tr. David Magarshack, 1950) The best definition of man is: a biped, ungrateful. (tr. Mirra Ginsburg, 1974)

text: To care only for well-being seems to me positively ill-bred. Whether it's good or bad, it is sometimes very pleasant, too, to smash things.
author: Fyodor Dostoevsky

text: Every man has some reminiscences which he would not tell to everyone, but only to his friends. He has others which he would not reveal even to his friends, but only to himself, and that in secret. But finally there are still others which a man is even afraid to tell himself, and every decent man has a considerable number of such things stored away. One can even say that the more decent he is, the greater the number of such things in his mind.
author: Fyodor Dostoevsky

text: I could never stand more than three months of dreaming at a time without feeling an irresistible desire to plunge into society. When my dreams had reached such a point of bliss that it became essential to embrace my fellows and all mankind immediately, I needed at least one human being at hand who actually existed. I always had to adjust my passionate desire to embrace humanity so that it might fall on a Tuesday.
author: Fyodor Dostoevsky

text: I'm the nastiest, most ridiculous, pettiest, stupidest, and most envious worm of all those living on earth who're no better than me in any way, but who, the devil knows why, never get embarrassed, while all my life I have to endure insults from every louse — that's my fate.
author: Fyodor Dostoevsky

text: And now once again I asked myself the question: do I love her? And once more I could not answer, that is to say, again, for the hundredth time, I answered that I hated her.
author: Fyodor Dostoevsky

text: A gentleman, even if he loses everything he owns, must show no emotion. Money must be so far beneath a gentleman that it is hardly worth troubling about.
author: Fyodor Dostoevsky

text: All is in a man's hands and he lets it all slip from cowardice. Taking a new step, uttering a new word is what they fear most.
author: Fyodor Dostoevsky
source: Variant translation: "Taking a new step, uttering a new word, is what people fear most."

text: Talking nonsense is man's only privilege that distinguishes him from all other organisms.
author: Fyodor Dostoevsky

text: Nothing in the world is harder than speaking the truth and nothing easier than flattery. If there’s the hundredth part of a false note in speaking the truth, it leads to a discord, and that leads to trouble. But if all, to the last note, is false in flattery, it is just as agreeable, and is heard not without satisfaction. And however coarse the flattery, at least half will be sure to seem true.
author: Fyodor Dostoevsky
source: Variant translation: Nothing in this world is harder than speaking the truth, nothing easier than flattery.

text: Accept suffering and achieve atonement through it — that is what you must do.
author: Fyodor Dostoevsky

text: Pain and suffering are always inevitable for a large intelligence and a deep heart. The really great men must, I think, have great sadness on Earth.
author: Fyodor Dostoevsky

text: The more cunning a man is, the less he suspects that he will be caught in a simple thing. The more cunning a man is, the simpler the trap he must be caught in.
author: Fyodor Dostoevsky

text: To kill someone for committing murder is a punishment incomparably worse than the crime itself. Murder by legal sentence is immeasurably more terrible than murder by brigands.
author: Fyodor Dostoevsky

text: A fool with a heart and no sense is just as unhappy as a fool with sense and no heart.
author: Fyodor Dostoevsky

text: Inventors and geniuses have almost always been looked on as no better than fools at the beginning of their career, and very frequently at the end of it also.
author: Fyodor Dostoevsky

text: There is something at the bottom of every new human thought, every thought of genius, which can never be communicated to others. There's something left which cannot be induced to emerge from your brain, and remains with you forever; and with it you will die, without communicating to anyone perhaps the most important of your ideas.
author: Fyodor Dostoevsky

text: For there are two sorts of mind: one that matters, and one that doesn't matter.
author: Fyodor Dostoevsky

text: It is better to be unhappy and know the worst, than to be happy in a fool's paradise!
author: Fyodor Dostoevsky

text: It's sometimes even good to be ridiculous, if not better: we can the sooner forgive each other, the sooner humble ourselves; we can't understand everything at once, we can't start right out with perfection! To achieve perfection, one must first begin by not understanding many things! And if we understand too quickly, we may not understand well.
author: Fyodor Dostoevsky

text: Oh, how hard it is to be the only one who knows the truth!
author: Fyodor Dostoevsky
source: I I am a ridiculous man. They call me a madman now. That would be a distinct rise in my social position were it not that they still regard me as being as ridiculous as ever. But that does not make me angry any more. They are all dear to me now even while they laugh at me — yes, even then they are for some reason particularly dear to me. I shouldn't have minded laughing with them — not at myself, of course, but because I love them — had I not felt so sad as I looked at them. I feel sad because they do not know the truth, whereas I know it. Oh, how hard it is to be the only man to know the truth! But they won't understand that. No, they will not understand. (tr. David Magarshack , 2005
source_section: The Dream of a Ridiculous Man (1877)

text: I gave up caring about anything, and all the problems disappeared.
author: Fyodor Dostoevsky
source_section: The Dream of a Ridiculous Man (1877)

text: Suddenly I noticed a star, and it gave me an idea: I decided to kill myself that night.
author: Fyodor Dostoevsky
source_section: The Dream of a Ridiculous Man (1877)

text: The world now seemed created for me alone: if I shot myself the world would cease to be at least for me. As soon as my consciousness is extinguished, the whole world will vanish too and become void like a phantom, for possibly all this world and all these people are only me myself.
author: Fyodor Dostoevsky
source_section: The Dream of a Ridiculous Man (1877)

text: Dreams seem to be spurred on not by reason but by desire, not by the head but by the heart.
author: Fyodor Dostoevsky
source_section: The Dream of a Ridiculous Man (1877)

text: Does it matter whether it was a dream or reality, if the dream made known to me the truth? If once one has recognized the truth and seen it, you know that it is the truth and that there is no other and there cannot be, whether you are asleep or awake. My dream revealed to me a different life, renewed, grand and full of power!
author: Fyodor Dostoevsky
source_section: The Dream of a Ridiculous Man (1877)

text: On our earth we can only love with suffering and through suffering. We cannot love otherwise, and we know of no other sort of love. I want suffering in order to love.
author: Fyodor Dostoevsky
source_section: The Dream of a Ridiculous Man (1877)

text: Their knowledge was gained and fostered by intuitions different from those of us on earth. They desired nothing and were at peace; they did not aspire to knowledge of life as we aspire to understand it, because their lives were full. Their knowledge was higher and deeper than ours; for our science seeks to explain what life is, aspires to understand it in order to teach others how to love, while they without science knew how to live.
author: Fyodor Dostoevsky
source_section: The Dream of a Ridiculous Man (1877)

text: It was like being in love with each other, but an all-embracing, universal feeling.
author: Fyodor Dostoevsky
source_section: The Dream of a Ridiculous Man (1877)

text: How can I help believing that it was all true? It was perhaps a thousand times brighter, happier and more joyful than I describe it. Granted that I dreamed it, yet it must have been real. Perhaps it was not a dream at all!
author: Fyodor Dostoevsky
source_section: The Dream of a Ridiculous Man (1877)

text: I only know that I was the cause of their sin and downfall. Like a vile trichina, like a germ of the plague infecting whole kingdoms, so I contaminated all this earth, so happy and sinless before my coming. They learnt to lie, grew fond of lying, and discovered the charm of falsehood.
author: Fyodor Dostoevsky
source_section: The Dream of a Ridiculous Man (1877)

text: All became so jealous of the rights of their own personality that they did their very utmost to curtail and destroy them in others. Slavery followed, even voluntary slavery; the weak eagerly submitted to the strong, on condition that the latter aided them to subdue the still weaker. Saints came to these people, weeping, and talked to them of their pride, of their loss of harmony and shame. They were laughed at or pelted with stones.
author: Fyodor Dostoevsky
source_section: The Dream of a Ridiculous Man (1877)

text: I yearned for suffering, longed for my blood to be drained to the last drop. But they only laughed at me, and began at last to look upon me as crazy. Then I awoke.
author: Fyodor Dostoevsky
source_section: The Dream of a Ridiculous Man (1877)

text: I go to spread the tidings — of the truth, for I have seen it, seen it with my own eyes, seen it in all its glory.
author: Fyodor Dostoevsky
source_section: The Dream of a Ridiculous Man (1877)

text: I have seen the truth: people can be beautiful and happy without losing the power of living on earth. I will not and cannot believe that evil is the normal condition of mankind. It is not as though I had invented it with my mind; I have seen it, and the living image of it has filled my soul forever.
author: Fyodor Dostoevsky
source_section: The Dream of a Ridiculous Man (1877)

text: What is a dream? And is not our life a dream? The chief thing is to love others like yourself, that's the chief thing, and that's everything. It's an old truth told a billion times, but it has not formed part of our lives! The consciousness of life is higher than life, the knowledge of the laws of happiness is higher than happiness — that is what one must contend against.
author: Fyodor Dostoevsky
source_section: The Dream of a Ridiculous Man (1877)

text: A man who lies to himself, and believes his own lies, becomes unable to recognize truth, either in himself or in anyone else, and he ends up losing respect for himself and for others. When he has no respect for anyone, he can no longer love, and in him, he yields to his impulses, indulges in the lowest form of pleasure, and behaves in the end like an animal in satisfying his vices. And it all comes from lying — to others and to yourself.
author: Fyodor Dostoevsky
source: Part I, Book I: A Nice Little Family, Ch. 2: The Old Buffoon (trans. Constance Garnett)

text: Men are made for happiness, and anyone who is completely happy has a right to say to himself, 'I am doing God's will on earth.' All the righteous, all the saints, all the holy martyrs were happy.
author: Fyodor Dostoevsky

text: I don't want harmony. From love for humanity I don't want it. I would rather be left with the unavenged suffering. Too high a price is asked for harmony; it's beyond our means to pay so much to enter on it. And so I hasten to give back my entrance ticket. It's not God that I don't accept, only I most respectfully return him the ticket.
author: Fyodor Dostoevsky
source: Book II, Chapter 4: Rebellion (trans. Constance Garnett)

text: 'I love humanity,' he said, 'but I wonder at myself. The more I love humanity in general, the less I love man in particular. I am incapable of living in the same room with any one for two days together. As soon as any one is near me, his personality disturbs my self-complacency and restricts my freedom. In twenty-four hours I begin to hate the best of men. But it has always happened that the more I detest men individually the more ardent becomes my love for humanity.'
author: Fyodor Dostoevsky

text: If you were to destroy in mankind the belief in immortality, not only love but every living force maintaining the life of the world would at once be dried up. Moreover, nothing then would be immoral, everything would be lawful, even cannibalism.
author: Fyodor Dostoevsky

text: How many meek and humble monks there are, yearning for solitude and fervent prayer in peace! From these meek monks, who yearn for solitary prayer, the salvation of Russia will come perhaps once more! For in their solitude, they keep the image of Christ fair and undefiled, in the purity of God's truth. And when the time comes they will show it to the tottering creeds of the world. That star will rise out of the East.
author: Fyodor Dostoevsky
source: Book VI, Chapter 3: Conversations and Exhortations of Father Zossima; The Russian Monk and his possible Significance (trans. Constance Garnett)

text: Love a man even in his sin, for that is the semblance of Divine Love and is the highest love on earth. Love all God's creation, the whole of it and every grain of sand in it. If you love everything, you will perceive the divine mystery in things, and come at last to love the world with an all-embracing love. Everything, like the ocean, flows and enters into contact with everything else: touch one place, and you set up a movement at the other end of the world. Treasure this ecstasy, however absurd people may think it.
author: Fyodor Dostoevsky
source: Book VI, Chapter 3: Conversations and Exhortations of Father Zossima; Of Prayer, of Love, and of Contact with other Worlds (trans. Constance Garnett)

text: I ponder, 'What is hell?' I maintain that it is the suffering of being unable to love.
author: Fyodor Dostoevsky

text: A beast can never be so cruel as a man, so artistically cruel. The tiger only tears and gnaws; he would never think of nailing people by the ears.
author: Fyodor Dostoevsky

text: I think the devil doesn't exist, but man has created him, he has created him in his own image and likeness.
author: Fyodor Dostoevsky

text: Even there, in the mines, underground, I may find a human heart in another convict and murderer by my side, for even there one may live and love and suffer. One may thaw and revive a frozen heart, and at last bring up from the dark depths a lofty soul, a feeling, suffering creature; one may bring forth an angel, create a hero!
author: Fyodor Dostoevsky

text: People talk sometimes of bestial cruelty, but that's a great injustice and insult to the beasts; a beast can never be so cruel as a man, so artistically cruel.
author: Fyodor Dostoevsky

text: Love in action is a harsh and dreadful thing compared with love in dreams. Love in dreams is greedy for immediate action, rapidly performed and in the sight of all. But active love is labour and fortitude, and for some people too, perhaps, a complete science. Just when you see with horror that in spite of all your efforts you are getting farther from your goal, at that very moment you will reach it and behold clearly the miraculous power of the Lord who has been all the time loving and mysteriously guiding you.
author: Fyodor Dostoevsky

text: Being in love doesn't mean loving. You may be in love with a woman and yet hate her.
author: Fyodor Dostoevsky

text: Beauty is a terrible and awful thing! It is terrible because it has not been fathomed and never can be fathomed, for God sets us nothing but riddles. Here the boundaries meet and all contradictions exist side by side. I can't endure the thought that a man of lofty mind and heart begins with the ideal of the Madonna and ends with the ideal of Sodom. What's still more awful is that a man with the ideal of Sodom in his soul does not renounce the ideal of the Madonna. What to the mind is shameful is beauty and nothing else to the heart. The awful thing is that beauty is mysterious as well as terrible. God and the devil are fighting there and the battlefield is the heart of man.
author: Fyodor Dostoevsky

text: Why count the days, when even one day is enough for a man to know all happiness?
author: Fyodor Dostoevsky

text: The degree of civilization in a society can be judged by entering its prisons.
author: Fyodor Dostoevsky
source: Alleged to be from House of the Dead , but no such quotation is present.

text: You read something which you thought only happened to you, and you discover that it happened 100 years ago to Dostoyevsky. This is a very great liberation for the suffering, struggling person, who always thinks that he is alone. This is why art is important.
author: Fyodor Dostoevsky

text: The real 19th century prophet was Dostoevsky, not Karl Marx.
author: Fyodor Dostoevsky

text: Dostoevsky, the only psychologist from whom I had something to learn.
author: Fyodor Dostoevsky
source: Friedrich Nietzsche in Twilight of the Idols (1889)

text: If God did not exist, everything would be permitted. Man is forlorn, for he cannot find anything to depend upon either within or outside himself. He discovers forthwith that he is without excuse. Man is free, man is freedom.
author: Fyodor Dostoevsky
source: Jean-Paul Sartre Existentialism and Humanism , 1948 p. 33-34

text: Dostoyevsky, patron saint of substance over style.
author: Fyodor Dostoevsky
source: Zadie Smith , from essay in the collection Changing My Mind (2009)

text: Major writers are usually those who have had to struggle against the odds, while writers who have had an easy start in life are usually second rate.
author: Fyodor Dostoevsky
source: Colin Wilson in The Books In My Life , p. 188

text: We are abandoned, like lost children in the woods. When you stand before me and look, what do you know of my pains, and what do I know of yours? Even if I were to weep and tell all, what more would you know of me than of hell, if someone merely told you it is hot and terrible? For this reason, we should stand before one another with such reverence, thoughtfulness, and love, as before the entrance to hell.
author: Franz Kafka
source: We are as forlorn as children lost in the woods. When you stand in front of me and look at me, what do you know of the griefs that are in me and what do I know of yours? And if I were to cast myself down before you and weep and tell you, what more would you know about me than you know about Hell when someone tells you it is hot and dreadful? For that reason alone we human beings ought to stand before one another as reverently, as reflectively, as lovingly, as we would before the entrance to Hell. Letter to Oskar Pollak (8 November 1903); cited from Briefe, 1902-1924 (1958) edited by [Max Brod]], p. 27 ; translation from Franz Kafka, Representative Man (1991) by Frederick R. Karl, p. 98

text: I think we ought to read only the kind of books that wound and stab us. If the book we're reading doesn't wake us with a blow to the head, what's the point of reading it? We need the books that affect us like a disaster, that grieve us deeply, like the death of someone we loved more than ourselves, like being banished into forests far from everyone, like a suicide. A book must be the axe for the frozen sea within us.
author: Franz Kafka
source: I think we ought to read only the kind of books that wound and stab us. If the book we are reading doesn't wake us up with a blow on the head, what are we reading it for? ...we need the books that affect us like a disaster, that grieve us deeply, like the death of someone we loved more than ourselves, like being banished into forests far from everyone, like a suicide. A book must be the axe for the frozen sea inside us. Letter to Oskar Pollak (27 January 1904)

text: The bliss of murder! The relief, the soaring ecstasy from the shedding of another’s blood! Why aren’t you simply a bladder of blood so that I could stamp on you and make you vanish into nothingness?
author: Franz Kafka

text: As Gregor Samsa awoke one morning from uneasy dreams, he found himself transformed in his bed into a monstrous vermin.
author: Franz Kafka
source: As Gregor Samsa awoke one morning from uneasy dreams he found himself transformed in his bed into an enormous insect . First lines

text: What a fate: to be condemned to work for a firm where the slightest negligence at once gave rise to the gravest suspicion!
author: Franz Kafka

text: How about if I sleep a little bit longer and forget all this nonsense.
author: Franz Kafka

text: Gregor tried to suppose to himself that what had happened to him might some day also happen to the chief clerk. There was no denying that anything was possible.
author: Franz Kafka

text: I cannot make you understand. I cannot make anyone understand what is happening inside me. I cannot even explain it to myself.
author: Franz Kafka

text: His conviction that he would have to disappear was, if possible, even firmer than his sister's. He remained in this state of empty and peaceful reflection until the tower clock struck three in the morning. He still saw that outside the window everything was beginning to grow light. Then, without his consent, his head sank down to the floor, and from his nostrils streamed his last weak breath.
author: Franz Kafka

text: Someone must have been telling lies about Joseph K., for without having done anything wrong he was arrested one fine morning.
author: Franz Kafka

text: You may object that it is not a trial at all; you are quite right, for it is only a trial if I recognize it as such.
author: Franz Kafka

text: The right understanding of any matter and a misunderstanding of the same matter do not wholly exclude each other.
author: Franz Kafka

text: While his case was unfolding itself, while up in the attics the Court officials were poring over the charge papers, was he to devote his attention to the affairs of the bank? It looked like a kind of torture sanctioned by the Court, arising from his case and concomitant with it.
author: Franz Kafka

text: Logic may indeed be unshakeable, but it cannot withstand a man who is determined to live.
author: Franz Kafka

text: "Don't you want to join us?" I was recently asked by an acquaintance when he ran across me alone after midnight in a coffeehouse that was already almost deserted. "No, I don't," I said.
author: Franz Kafka

text: Germany has declared war on Russia. Swimming in the afternoon.
author: Franz Kafka
source: Diary entry for August 2nd, 1914, quoted in "Fighting a private war" , Irish Times (Oct 20 2001)

text: It is entirely conceivable that life’s splendour forever lies in wait about each one of us in all its fullness, but veiled from view, deep down, invisible, far off. It is there, though, not hostile, not reluctant, not deaf. If you summon it by the right word, by its right name, it will come. This is the essence of magic, which does not create but summons.
author: Franz Kafka

text: Anyone who cannot come to terms with his life while he is alive needs one hand to ward off a little his despair over his fate — he has little success in this — but with his other hand he can note down what he sees among the ruins, for he sees different (and more) things than do the others; after all, dead as he is in his own lifetime, he is the real survivor.
author: Franz Kafka

text: It is perhaps not truly love when I say that you are dearest to me; love is that you are the knife with which I dig in myself.
author: Franz Kafka
source: Aren’t our eyes made to be torn out, and our hearts for the same purpose? At the same time it’s really not that bad; that’s an exaggeration and a lie, everything is exaggeration, the only truth is longing, which cannot be exaggerated. But even the truth of longing is not so much its own truth; it’s really an expression of everything else, which is a lie. This sounds crazy and distorted, but it’s true. Moreover, perhaps it isn’t love when I say you are what I love the most — you are the knife I turn inside myself, this is love. Letter to Milena Jesenská (14 September 1920)

text: The thornbush is old obstacle in the road. It must catch fire if you want to go further.
author: Franz Kafka

text: Anyone who believes cannot experience miracles. By day one does not see any stars.
author: Franz Kafka

text: Evil knows about good, but good does not know about evil. Only evil has self-knowledge.
author: Franz Kafka
source: Translation: Evil knows of the Good, but Good does not know of Evil. Knowledge of oneself is something only Evil has. - The First Octavo Notebook

text: Now at last I can look at you in peace, I don't eat you anymore.
author: Franz Kafka
source: Comment to a fish, after becoming a vegetarian, p. 74

text: Everything you say is boring and incomprehensible, but that alone doesn't make it true.
author: Franz Kafka

text: Even remembering in itself is sad, yet how much more its object! It only weakens one’s present position without strengthening the former one.
author: Franz Kafka

text: It was not the hunger artist who was cheating, he was working honestly, but the world was cheating him of his reward.
author: Franz Kafka

text: To fight against this lack of understanding, against a whole world of non-understanding, was impossible.
author: Franz Kafka

text: I couldn't find the food I liked. If I had found it, believe me, I should have made no fuss and stuffed myself like you or anyone else. These were his last words, but in his dimming eyes remained the firm though no longer proud persuasion that he was still continuing to fast.
author: Franz Kafka

text: From the very beginning I sensed some discrepancy, some little maladjustment, causing a slight feeling of discomfort which not even the most decorous public functions could eliminate; more, the mere look of some fellow dog would fill me with helpless embarrassment and fear, even with despair.
author: Franz Kafka

text: All knowledge, the totality of all questions and all answers, is contained in the dog. If we dogs would but own that we know infinitely more than we admit to ourselves!
author: Franz Kafka

text: "You asking me the way?" "Yes," I said, "since I can't find it myself." "Give it up! Give it up!" said he, and turned with a sudden jerk, like someone who wants to be alone with his laughter.
author: Franz Kafka
source: Variant translation: The Policeman said to me, "You want to know the way? Give up! Just give up!" And he turned away like a man that wants to be alone with his laughter.

text: Behind them already are the secretaries, officials, professional politicians, all the modern satraps for whom they are preparing the way to power. At the end of every truly revolutionary development there appears a Napoleon Bonaparte. As a flood spreads wider and wider, the water becomes shallower and dirtier. The Revolution evaporates, and leaves behind only the slime of a new bureaucracy. The chains of tormented mankind are made out of red tape.
author: Franz Kafka
source: Gustav Janouch, Conversations With Kafka: Notes and Reminiscences (1953), page 71, London: Derek Verschoyle; frequently quoted as " Every revolution evaporates, and leaves behind only the slime of a new bureaucracy."

text: Don't bend; don't water it down; don't try to make it logical; don't edit your own soul according to the fashion. Rather, follow your most intense obsessions mercilessly.
author: Franz Kafka
source: Attributed to Kafka by numerous sources, confirmed to be from Anne Rice . [ 1 ]

text: One idiot is one idiot. Two idiots are two idiots. Ten thousand idiots are a political party.
author: Franz Kafka
source: Was written in a slightly different way by Leo Longanesi in Italian, above form has been attributed to Kafka without evidence. [ 2 ]

text: He is interested in the feelings of the squash ball, and of the champagne bottle that launches the ship. In a football match his sympathy is not with either of the teams but with the ball, or, in a match ending nil-nil, with the hunger of the goalmouth.
author: Franz Kafka

text: Treat a man as sub-human, and we make it easier for ourselves to eliminate him with an unstained conscience.
author: Franz Kafka
source: Michael Billington , 'Unnerving account', The Times (16 April 1969), p. 13

text: Kafka described with wonderful imaginative power the future concentration camps, the future instability of the law, the future absolutism of the state Apparat.
author: Franz Kafka
source: Bertolt Brecht , as quoted in Time (18 July 1983)

text: Literature gives you: the reverse side of history.
author: Franz Kafka

text: When I first read Kafka, I constantly had the feeling that I was writing it myself. It was as if I'd had a similar basic experience of the world.
author: Franz Kafka
source: Václav Havel , quoted in 'Václav Havel', The Times (19 December 2011), p. 49

text: Franz Kafka has become emblematic of the horrors of our century; the word 'Kafkaesque' has entered the language.
author: Franz Kafka
source: Daniel Johnson , 'Is this the best tale of the century', The Times (30 December 1995), p. 20

text: Maybe talking down to yourself is a way of keeping the faith.
author: Franz Kafka

text: I didn't know anyone was allowed to write things like that. If I had known, I would have started writing a long time ago.
author: Franz Kafka

text: Kafka, the sickly, alienated individualist, the Jew who never completely felt himself to be a citizen of the Jewish, the Czech, or the German worlds, has risen from the dead in the vulgarized form of a sort of Czech rock star.
author: Franz Kafka
source: Chava Rosenfarb "Laterna Magika, Prague 1993" in Confessions of a Yiddish Writer and Other Essays , translated from the Yiddish with Goldie Morgentaler

text: Franz Kafka described the workings of the communist state's impersonal machine in a prophetic book, the moral of which many statesmen have yet to learn.
author: Franz Kafka
source: Roger Scruton , 'Responses from the house of the dead', The Times (4 October 1983), p. 10

text: With their posterior legs they were still glued to their father's Jewishness, and with their waving anterior legs they found no new ground. Kafka's Jewish question ('What have I in common with Jews?') has become everybody's question, Jewish alienation the template for all our doubts. These days we all find our anterior legs flailing before us. We're all insects, all Ungeziefer, now.
author: Franz Kafka
source: Zadie Smith , from essay in the collection Changing My Mind (2009)

text: Kafka idealized Galician Jewish refugees as the embodiment of authenticity, writing that if he could be anybody, he’d want to be a little Jewish boy he remembered seeing, seemingly free of worry. We’re always trying to deprogram ourselves from what we have learned as authenticity when we were young.
author: Franz Kafka

text: It's 4:30 in the morning, it's always 4:30 in the morning.
author: Charles Bukowski

text: The impossibility of being human, all too human, moving this little bit of light toward us impossibly.
author: Charles Bukowski

text: I've never met another man I'd rather be.
author: Charles Bukowski

text: I walk through rooms of the dead, streets of the dead, cities of the dead: men without eyes, men without voices; men with manufactured feelings and standard reactions; men with newspaper brains, television souls and high school ideals.
author: Charles Bukowski
source: in Sunlight Here I Am: Interviews and Encounters, 1963-1993 (2003), p. 24

text: If you want to know who your friends are, get yourself a jail sentence.
author: Charles Bukowski
source_section: Notes of a Dirty Old Man (1969)

text: An intellectual is a man who says a simple thing in a difficult way; an artist is a man who says a difficult thing in a simple way.
author: Charles Bukowski
source_section: Notes of a Dirty Old Man (1969)

text: Show me a man who lives alone and has a perpetually clean kitchen, and eight times out of nine I'll show you a man with detestable spiritual qualities.
author: Charles Bukowski

text: The free soul is rare, but you know it when you see it - basically because you feel good, very good, when you are near or with them.
author: Charles Bukowski

text: Any damn fool can beg up some kind of job; it takes a wise man to make it without working.
author: Charles Bukowski

text: I wanted the whole world or nothing.
author: Charles Bukowski

text: Women were meant to suffer; no wonder they asked for constant declarations of love.
author: Charles Bukowski

text: I was a man who thrived on solitude; without it I was like another man without food or water. Each day without solitude weakened me. I took no pride in my solitude; but I was dependent on it. The darkness of the room was like sunlight to me.
author: Charles Bukowski

text: Love is for real people. I dislike real people. I hate them.
author: Charles Bukowski

text: That was all a man needed: hope. It was a lack of hope that discouraged a man. The myth of the starving artist was a hoax.
author: Charles Bukowski

text: Frankly, I was horrified by life, at what a man had to do simply in order to eat, sleep, and keep himself clothed. So I stayed in bed and drank. When you drank the world was still out there, but for the moment it didn't have you by the throat.
author: Charles Bukowski

text: I'm a genius but nobody knows it but me.
author: Charles Bukowski

text: When they demonstrate that the world has four dimensions instead of just three, a man will be able to go for a walk and just disappear. No burial, no tears, no illusions, no heaven or hell.
author: Charles Bukowski

text: My ambition is handicapped by my laziness.
author: Charles Bukowski

text: I've given you my time. It's all I've got to give - it's all any man has. If anybody has lost anything on this deal, I've been the loser.
author: Charles Bukowski

text: People don't need love. What they need is success in one form or another. It can be love but it needn't be.
author: Charles Bukowski

text: How in the hell could a man enjoy being awakened at 6:30 a.m. by an alarm clock, leap out of bed, dress, force-feed, shit, piss, brush teeth and hair, and fight traffic to get to a place where essentially you made lots of money for somebody else and were asked to be grateful for the opportunity to do so?
author: Charles Bukowski

text: With one error of judgment, he'll kill us all. He could do it. Dump us all. I knew that if I was driving that I would consider the possibility or desirability of drowning everybody. And sometimes, after just such considerations, possibility turns into reality. For each Joan of Arc there is a Hitler perched at the other end of the teeter-totter. Yet, they were thinking instead of car payments, baseball scores, haircuts, vacations, enemas, family visits. There wasn't a real man in the whole shitload.
author: Charles Bukowski

text: Even the most horrible human being on earth deserves to wipe his ass.
author: Charles Bukowski

text: Like every American boy I had always been told: catch cancer early. Then you go down to catch it early and they make you wait three weeks for an appointment. That's the difference between what we're told and actuality.
author: Charles Bukowski

text: The bums lived down there by the hundreds... All they needed to live like kings was canned heat and what they picked out of the nearby garbage dump. They were tan and relaxed and most of them looked a hell of a lot healthier than the average Los Angeles business man. Those guys down there had no problems with women, income tax, landlords, burial expenses, dentists, time payments, car repairs, or with climbing into a voting booth and pulling the curtain closed.
author: Charles Bukowski

text: There were worse things than looking for a job you didn't want.
author: Charles Bukowski

text: The lives that people lead are driving them crazy and their insanity comes out in the way they drive.
author: Charles Bukowski

text: Almost everybody was a writer. Not everybody thought they could be a dentist or an automobile mechanic but everybody knew they could be a writer. But most men, fortunately, aren't writers, or even cab drivers, and some men - many men - unfortunately aren't anything.
author: Charles Bukowski

text: People in love often become edgy, dangerous. They lose their sense of perspective. They lose their sense of humor. They become nervous, psychotic bores. They even become killers.
author: Charles Bukowski

text: Human relationships didn't work anyhow. Masks dropped away and real people began to appear: cranks, imbeciles, the demented, the vengeful, sadists, killers. Modern society had created its own kind and they feasted on each other. It was a duel to the death--in a cesspool.
author: Charles Bukowski

text: People with no morals often considered themselves more free, but mostly they lacked the ability to feel hate or love.
author: Charles Bukowski

text: Morals were restrictive, but they were grounded on human experience.
author: Charles Bukowski

text: Many a good man has been put under the bridge by a woman.
author: Charles Bukowski

text: Once a woman turns against you, forget it. They can love you, then something turns in them. They can watch you dying in a gutter, run over by a car, and they'll spit on you.
author: Charles Bukowski

text: I was drawn to all the wrong things: I liked to drink, I was lazy, I didn't have a god, politics, ideas, ideals. I was settled into nothingness; a kind of non-being, and I accepted it. I didn't want to be interesting, it was too hard. What I really wanted was only a soft, hazy space to live in, and to be left alone. Yet, when I got drunk I screamed, went crazy, got all out of hand. One kind of behavior didn't fit the other. I didn't care.
author: Charles Bukowski

text: Nothing was ever in tune. People just blindly grabbed at whatever there was: communism, health foods, zen, surfing, ballet, hypnotism, group encounters, orgies, biking, herbs, Catholicism, weight-lifting, travel, withdrawal, vegetarianism, India, painting, writing, sculpting, composing, conducting, backpacking, yoga, copulating, gambling, drinking, hanging around, frozen yogurt, Beethoven, Bach, Buddha, Christ, TM, H, carrot juice, suicide, handmade suits, jet travel, New York City, and then it all evaporated and fell apart. People had to find things to do while waiting to die. I guess it was nice to have a choice.
author: Charles Bukowski

text: All a guy needed was a chance. Somebody was always controlling who got a chance and who didn’t.
author: Charles Bukowski

text: Drink was the only thing that kept a man from feeling forever stunned and useless. Everything else just kept picking and picking, hacking away. And nothing was interesting, nothing. The people were restrictive and careful, all alike. They shit and they chattered and they were dull as horse dung. But get up close and listen to their minds running out of their mouths, you felt like digging in under a hill and hiding out with a tommy-gun. I would certainly never be able to be happy, to get married, I could never have children.
author: Charles Bukowski

text: The problem was you had to keep choosing between one evil or another, and no matter what you chose, they sliced a little more off you, until there was nothing left. At the age of 25 most people were finished. I had no interests. I had no interest in anything. I had no idea how I was going to escape. At least the others had some taste for life. They seemed to understand something that I didn't understand. Maybe I was lacking. It was possible. I often felt inferior. I just wanted to get away from them. But there was no place to go.
author: Charles Bukowski

text: Money is like sex. It seems much more important when you don't have any...
author: Charles Bukowski

text: There's a bluebird in my heart that wants to get out but I'm too tough for him, I say, stay in there, I'm not going to let anybody see you. I only let him out at night sometimes when everybody's asleep. He's singing a little in there, I haven't quite let him die. And it's nice enough to make a man weep, but I don't weep, do you?
author: Charles Bukowski
source_section: The Last Night of the Earth Poems (1992)

text: A woman can drop out of your life and forget you real fast. A woman can't go anywhere but UP after leaving you, honey.
author: Charles Bukowski
source_section: The Last Night of the Earth Poems (1992)

text: Sometimes I felt that I didn’t even know who I was. I could be anybody, what does it matter?
author: Charles Bukowski

text: Man was born to die. What did it mean? Hanging around and waiting. Waiting for the ‘A train.’ Waiting for a pair of big breasts on some August night in a Vegas hotel room. Waiting for the mouse to sing. Waiting for the snake to grow wings. Hanging around.
author: Charles Bukowski

text: Sex was a trap, a snare. It was for animals.
author: Charles Bukowski

text: Something was always after a man. It never relented. No rest, ever.
author: Charles Bukowski

text: I am waiting to live, waiting to die. I wish I could ring in some bravery.
author: Charles Bukowski
source: Lines from "So now?" - p.402 (circa 1994. He died in March 1994, aged 73.)
source_section: Betting on the Muse: Poems and Stories (1996)

text: There's nothing to mourn about death any more than there is to mourn about the growing of a flower. What is terrible is not death but the lives people live or don't live up until their death. They don't honor their own lives, they piss on their lives. They shit them away. Dumb fuckers. They concentrate too much on fucking, movies, money, family, fucking. Their minds are full of cotton. They swallow God without thinking, they swallow country without thinking. Soon they forget how to think, they let others think for them. Their brains are stuffed with cotton. They look ugly, they talk ugly, they walk ugly. Play them the great music of the centuries and they can't hear it. Most people's deaths are a sham. There's nothing left to die.
author: Charles Bukowski
source_section: The Captain is Out to Lunch and the Sailors have taken over the Ship (1998)

text: We're all going to die, all of us, what a circus! That alone should make us love each other but it doesn't. We are terrorized and flattened by trivialities, we are eaten up by nothing.
author: Charles Bukowski
source_section: The Captain is Out to Lunch and the Sailors have taken over the Ship (1998)

text: Don't wait for the good woman. She doesn't exist. There are women who can make you feel more with their bodies and their souls but these are the exact women who will turn the knife into you right in front of the crowd. Of course, I expect this, but the knife still cuts. The female loves to play man against man, and if she is in a position to do it there is not one who will not resist. The male, for all his bravado and exploration, is the loyal one, the one who generally feels love. The female is skilled at betrayal and torture and damnation. Never envy a man his lady. Behind it all lays a living hell.
author: Charles Bukowski
source: in a letter to Steven Richmond (Published in Charles Bukowski: Locked in the Arms of a Crazy Life by Howard Sounes)

text: If I want to kill myself I feel that should be my business. If I go out and hold up gas stations at night to pay for my supply it is because the law inflates a very cheap thing into an escalated war against my nerves and my soul.
author: Charles Bukowski
source: "This Floundering Old Bastard is the Best Damn Poet in Town", interview by John Thomas, in LA Free Press (1967)

text: If I'm an ass, I should say so. If I don't, somebody else will. If I say it first, that disarms them.
author: Charles Bukowski

text: For those who believe in God, most of the big questions are answered. But for those of us who can't readily accept the God formula, the big answers don't remain stonewritten. We adjust to new conditions and discoveries. We are pliable. Love need not be a command or faith a dictum. I am my own God. We are here to unlearn the teachings of the church, state and our educational system. We are here to drink beer. We are here to kill war. We are here to laugh at the odds and live our lives so well that Death will tremble to take us.
author: Charles Bukowski
source: "The Meaning of Life: The Big Picture", Life Magazine (December 1988)

text: I owed to my nature as a Jew alone the two qualities that had become indispensable to me in the course of my difficult life. As a Jew, I found myself free of many of those prejudices that limit other men in the use of their intellect and, as a Jew, I found myself ready to go over to the opposition and to renounce agreement with the 'silent majority'.
author: Sigmund Freud
source: Mi convinsi ben presto che dovevo solo alla mia natura di ebreo le due qualità che mi erano diventate indispensabili nel corso della mia vita difficile. Essendo ebreo mi trovavo libero da molti di quel pregiudizi che limitano gli altri uomini nell'uso del proprio intelletto e, in quanto ebreo, mi trovavo pronto a passare all'opposizione e a rinunciare a un accordo con la "maggioranza silenziosa". Così divenni uno dei vostri; partecipai ai vostri interessi umanitari e nazionali, mi feci degli amici tra di voi e in seguito convinsi i pochi amici che mi restavano (il Dr. Hitschmarm e il Dr. Rie) ad associarsi a voi. Non è che volessi conquistarvi ai miei insegnamenti, in un'epoca in cui in Europa nessuno mi ascoltava, voi mi accordaste una benevola attenzione. Voi foste il mio primo uditorio. As quoted in Emmanuel Ratier , Misteri e segreti del B'nai B'rith , Centro Studi Sadalitium, 2014. OCLC 799225112.

text: How bold one gets when one is sure of being loved.
author: Sigmund Freud
source: Letter to his fiancée Martha Bernays (27 June 1882); published in Letters of Sigmund Freud 1873-1939 (1961), 10-12

text: A man like me cannot live without a hobby-horse, a consuming passion — in Schiller's words a tyrant. I have found my tyrant, and in his service I know no limits.
author: Sigmund Freud
source: Ein Mensch wie ich kann ohne Steckenpferd, ohne herrschende Leidenschaften, ohne einen Tyrannen in Schillers Worten, nicht leben. Ich habe meinen Tyrannen gefunden und in seinem Dienst kenne ich kein Maß.

text: Much has been gained if we succeed in turning your hysterical misery into common unhappiness.
author: Sigmund Freud
source: Studies on Hysteria (1895), (co-written with Josef Breuer ) as translated by Nicola Luckhurst (2004)

text: Being entirely honest with oneself is a good exercise.
author: Sigmund Freud
source: Letter to Wilhelm Fliess (15 October 1897), as quoted in Origins of Psychoanalysis

text: A woman is to soften but not weaken a man.
author: Sigmund Freud

text: I am by temperament nothing but a conquistador — an adventurer, if you want it translated — with all the curiosity, daring, and tenacity characteristic of a man of this sort.
author: Sigmund Freud
source: Letter to Wilhelm Fliess, Feb. 1, 1900. The Complete Letters of Sigmund Freud to Wilhelm Fliess 1887-1904 (1985).

text: The interpretation of dreams is the royal road to a knowledge of the unconscious activities of the mind.
author: Sigmund Freud
source: The Interpretation of Dreams (1900), from The Standard Edition of the Complete Psychological Works of Sigmund Freud , translated by James Strachey.

text: No one who, like me, conjures up the most evil of those half-tamed demons that inhabit the human beast, and seeks to wrestle with them, can expect to come through the struggle unscathed.
author: Sigmund Freud
source: Dora : An Analysis of a Case of Hysteria (1905), his analysis of the case of Ida Bauer (also translated as Fragment of an Analysis of a Case of Hysteria )

text: He that has eyes to see and ears to hear may convince himself that no mortal can keep a secret. If his lips are silent, he chatters with his fingertips; betrayal oozes out of him at every pore.
author: Sigmund Freud
source: Fragment of an Analysis of a Case of Hysteria (1905) Ch. 2 : The First Dream

text: Psychoanalysis is in essence a cure through love.
author: Sigmund Freud
source: Letter to Carl Jung (1906), as quoted in Freud and Man's Soul (1984) by Bruno Bettelheim

text: The virtuous man contents himself with dreaming that which the wicked man does in actual life.
author: Sigmund Freud
source: Quoting Plato, as translated by Abraham Arden Brill, "The Interpretation of Dreams" (1913 edition), p.493

text: Conscience is the internal perception of the rejection of a particular wish operating within us.
author: Sigmund Freud
source: Totem and Taboo: Resemblances Between the Mental Lives of Savages and Neurotics (1913)

text: At bottom God is nothing more than an exalted father.
author: Sigmund Freud
source: Totem and Taboo : Resemblances Between the Mental Lives of Savages and Neurotics (1913)

text: To have been the undisputed favorite of one's mother is to carry through life a conqueror's spirit, an unwavering confidence in success, which often, indeed, brings success in its wake.
author: Sigmund Freud
source: Eine Kindheitserinnerung aus »Dichtung und Wahrheit« , first published in the journal Imago, vol. 5 issue 2 (1917), p. 57 books.google = http://www.gutenberg.org/files/29946/29946-h/29946-h.htm

text: We are and remain Jews. The others will only exploit us and will never understand and appreciate us.
author: Sigmund Freud

text: Biology is a land of unlimited possibilities, whose future answers may blow away the whole of our artificial structure of hypothesis.
author: Sigmund Freud

text: Cruelty and intolerance to those who do not belong to it are natural to every religion.
author: Sigmund Freud
source: Group Psychology and the Analysis of the Ego (1921)

text: To be in love is to be humble. To love is to shed a piece of one's narcissism.
author: Sigmund Freud
source: Whoever loves become humble. Those who love have, so to speak, pawned a part of their narcissism .

text: When the wayfarer whistles in the dark, he may be disavowing his timidity, but he does not see any more clearly for doing so.
author: Sigmund Freud

text: The ego represents what we call reason and sanity, in contrast to the id which contains the passions.
author: Sigmund Freud

text: The ego, in its relation to the id, is like a rider upon a horse: it must hold in check the superior strength of the beast, yet often finds itself obliged to guide it where it wants to go, transforming the id's will into action as if it were its own.
author: Sigmund Freud
source: (p.25 in The Standard Edition, Ed. James Strachey)

text: If the truth of religious doctrines is dependent on an inner experience that bears witness to the truth, what is one to make of the many people who do not have that experience?
author: Sigmund Freud

text: The voice of the intellect is soft, yet it does not rest until it has gained a hearing. Ultimately, after endless rebuffs, it succeeds.
author: Sigmund Freud

text: A culture that leaves so many unsatisfied and drives them to rebellion neither has a prospect of enduring nor deserves to.
author: Sigmund Freud
source: It goes without saying that a civilization which leaves so large a number of its participants unsatisfied and drives them into revolt neither has nor deserves the prospect of a lasting existence.

text: Religious ideas have sprung from the same need as all the other achievements of culture: from the necessity for defending itself against the crushing supremacy of nature.
author: Sigmund Freud

text: A poor girl may dream a prince will come and fetch her home. That the Messiah will come and found a golden age is much less probable.
author: Sigmund Freud

text: Religious doctrines are all illusions; they do not admit of proof, and no one can be compelled to consider them as true or to believe in them.
author: Sigmund Freud

text: Where the questions of religion are concerned people are guilty of every possible kind of insincerity and intellectual misdemeanor.
author: Sigmund Freud

text: Immorality, no less than morality, has at all times found support in religion.
author: Sigmund Freud

text: The true believer is protected against certain neurotic afflictions; by accepting the universal neurosis, he is spared the task of forming a personal neurosis.
author: Sigmund Freud

text: Religion is a childhood neurosis that mankind will surmount, just as children outgrow theirs.
author: Sigmund Freud

text: Religion is a system of wishful illusions together with a disavowal of reality, such as we find nowhere else but in a state of blissful hallucinatory confusion. Religion's eleventh commandment is "Thou shalt not question."
author: Sigmund Freud

text: Man's helplessness remains, and with it his longing for his father and the gods. The gods retain their threefold task: to exorcise the terrors of nature, reconcile men to the cruelty of Fate and death, and compensate them for the sufferings of civilized life.
author: Sigmund Freud

text: One cannot escape the impression that people commonly measure with false standards, striving for power, success, and wealth, while underestimating life's true values.
author: Sigmund Freud
source: It is impossible to escape the impression that people commonly use false standards of measurement — that they seek power , success and wealth for themselves and admire them in others, and that they underestimate what is of true value in life . Ch. 1, as translated by James Strachey , p.25

text: At the height of being in love, the boundary between ego and object threatens to melt away. Against all evidence, a man in love declares that 'I' and 'you' are one, and behaves as if it were a fact.
author: Sigmund Freud
source: Ch. 1, as translated by Joan Riviere (1961)

text: One feels inclined to say that the intention that man should be "happy" is not included in the plan of "Creation."
author: Sigmund Freud
source: Ch. 2, as translated by James Strachey , p.53

text: Beauty has no obvious use; nor is there any clear cultural necessity for it. Yet civilization could not do without it.
author: Sigmund Freud
source: Ch. 2, as translated by James Strachey , p.62

text: We are never so defenceless against suffering as when we love.
author: Sigmund Freud
source: Ch. 2; as translated by James Strachey , p.63

text: Men are not gentle creatures who want to be loved; they are, on the contrary, creatures among whose instinctual endowments is a powerful share of aggressiveness. Homo homini lupus.
author: Sigmund Freud
source: Ch. 2, as translated by James Strachey , p.68-69

text: The first requisite of civilization, therefore, is that of justice—that is, the assurance that a law once made will not be broken in favour of an individual.
author: Sigmund Freud
source: Ch. 3, as translated by James Strachey , p.81

text: Aggressiveness was not created by property. In abolishing private property, we deprive human aggression of one instrument, but we do not alter its nature.
author: Sigmund Freud
source: Ch. 5, as translated by James Strachey and Anna Freud (1961)

text: It is always possible to bind together a considerable number of people in love, so long as there are other people left over to receive manifestations of their aggressiveness.
author: Sigmund Freud
source: Ch. 5, as translated by James Strachey and Anna Freud (1961)

text: What progress we are making. In the Middle Ages they would have burned me. Now they are content with burning my books.
author: Sigmund Freud
source: Letter to Ernest Jones (1933), as quoted in The Columbia Dictionary of Quotations (1993) by Robert Andrews, p. 779

text: Every normal person is only normal on the average. His ego approximates to that of the psychotic in some part or other.
author: Sigmund Freud
source: Analysis Terminable and Interminable , sect. 5 (1937); reprinted in Complete Works, Standard Edition , vol. 23 (ed. James Strachey and Anna Freud. 1964); as quoted in The New Penguin Dictionary of Modern Quotations by Robert Andrews, Penguin Books, 2001.

text: The poet's derisive comment on the philosopher is not unjustified: 'With his nightcaps and the tatters of his dressing-gown he patches the gaps in the structure of the universe.'
author: Sigmund Freud

text: Analogies prove nothing, that is quite true, but they can make one feel more at home.
author: Sigmund Freud

text: The relation of the ego to the id is like that between a rider and his horse. The rider determines the goal, but all too often, the rider is obliged to guide his horse in the direction it itself wants to go.
author: Sigmund Freud
source: The Anatomy of the Mental Personality (Lecture 31)

text: The poor ego serves three harsh masters: the external world, the superego, and the id.
author: Sigmund Freud
source: The Anatomy of the Mental Personality (Lecture 31)

text: Thinking is an experimental dealing with small quantities of energy, just as a general moves miniature figures over a map before setting his troops in action.
author: Sigmund Freud

text: Religion is an attempt to get control over the sensory world, in which we are placed, by means of the wish-world, which we have developed inside us as a result of biological and psychological necessities.
author: Sigmund Freud

text: Religion is an illusion and it derives its strength from the fact that it falls in with our instinctual desires.
author: Sigmund Freud

text: Neuroses are not unnecessary ailments to be easily cured, but severe, constitutionally fixed illnesses that persist throughout life.
author: Sigmund Freud

text: The conscious mind may be compared to a fountain playing in the sun and falling back into the great subterranean pool of subconscious from which it rises.
author: Sigmund Freud
source: As quoted in his obituary, in the New York Times , 24 September, 1939

text: America is a mistake, admittedly a gigantic mistake, but a mistake nevertheless.
author: Sigmund Freud
source: Remark to Ernest Jones as quoted in The Life and Work of Sigmund Freud: Years of maturity, 1901-1919‎ (1957) by Ernest Jones, p. 60

text: A certain degree of neurosis is of inestimable value as a drive, especially to a psychologist .
author: Sigmund Freud
source: Fragments of an Analysis with Freud, ch.3 '22 January 1935' (1954) by Joseph Wortis; as quoted in Penguin Dictionary of Modern Quotations by Robert Andrews, Penguin Books, 2001.

text: I have found little 'good' about human beings; most are trash, regardless of their ethical doctrines. This is something one cannot say aloud, or perhaps even think.
author: Sigmund Freud
source: Psycho-analysis and faith: the letters of Sigmund Freud & Oskar Pfister (1963 edition)

text: Everywhere I go I find that a poet has been there before me.
author: Sigmund Freud
source: As quoted in In factor of the sensitive man, and other essays (1976 edition) by Anais Nin, p.14

text: Dogs love their friends and bite their enemies, quite unlike people, who are incapable of pure love and always have to mix love and hate in their object-relations.
author: Sigmund Freud
source: As quoted by Anna Freud in the preface to the (1981) edition of Topsy: The Story of a Golden-Haired Chow by Princess Marie Bonaparte .

text: I haven't discovered much 'good' in men; for the most part, they are nothing but scoundrels.
author: Sigmund Freud
source: Correspondance avec le pasteur Pfister, 1909-1939 , Gallimard, 1991, p.103; as quoted in Altruism: The Power of Compassion to Change Yourself and the World by Matthieu Ricard

text: A fear of weapons is a sign of retarded sexual and emotional maturity.
author: Sigmund Freud
source: This is not a statement that has been found in any translation of any of Freud's known works. It is a paraphrase of a statement from the essay "Guns, Murders, and the Constitution" (February 1990) by Don B. Kates, Jr. where Kates summarizes his views of passages in Dreams in Folklore (1958) by Freud and David E. Oppenheim, while disputing statements by Emmanuel Tanay in "Neurotic Attachment to Guns" in a 1976 edition of The Fifty Minute Hour: A Collection of True Psychoanalytic Tales (1955) by Robert Mitchell Lindner:

text: The idea of God is a device of the unconscious, an exalted father-figure born from infantile yearnings for protection and eternal life, a projection of desires worshiped out of helplessness. Religion, a necessary stage in humanity's infancy, should now be left behind.
author: Sigmund Freud
source: Summary of Freud's view found in Karen Armstrong's 'A History of God' (1993), p. 409

text: Women oppose change, receive passively, and add nothing of their own
author: Sigmund Freud
source: Alledgedly written in 'The Psychical Consequences of the Anatomic Distinction Between the Sexes', but Freud neither says this nor argues this exact sentiment. Possible originates from Donna Stewart

text: The child I carry for nine months can be defined neither as me nor as not-me. Far from existing in the mode of 'inner' space, women are powerfully attuned both to 'inner' and 'outer' because for us the two are continuous, not polar.
author: Sigmund Freud
source: Bettina Aptheker Tapestries of Life: Women's Work, Women's Consciousness, and the Meaning of Daily Experience (1989)

text: If often he was wrong and at times absurd To us he is no more a person Now but a climate of opinion .
author: Sigmund Freud
source: W. H. Auden , in "In Memory of Sigmund Freud" (1940)

text: Man’s depravity is rooted much deeper in his nature; the abolition of private property would do little to change his basic constitution. Socialism has its roots not in love and fraternity, but rather in revenge and aggression. It is always possible to bind together a considerable number of people in love, so long as there are other people left over to receive the manifestations of their aggressiveness.
author: Sigmund Freud
source: Nicholas Buccola, in "'The Tyranny of the Least and the Dumbest': Nietzsche’s Critique of Socialism” in Quarterly Journal of Ideology Vol 31, no. 3 & 4 (2004), quoting and summarizing Freud’s Civilization and Its Discontents

text: Methods presumed to discover what is in the unconscious often use symbolism and analogy such that the interpreter can find virtually anything he is looking for.
author: Sigmund Freud
source: Hervey Cleckley , The Mask of Sanity , 1941, fifth edition 1976, ISBN 0-9621519-0-4

text: Freud can hardly be regarded as a scientist but rather as a physician who founded the new cult of psychoanalysis.
author: Sigmund Freud
source: Francis Crick , The Astonishing Hypothesis: The Scientific Search for the Soul (1994)

text: A decade would pass before Freud would have his revenge and see his ideas begin to destroy sex in America forever.
author: Sigmund Freud
source: E. L. Doctorow , in Ragtime: A Novel (1976)

text: A special reserve of my anger was directed at Freud (formerly one of my heroes) for having labeled women "neurotic" when they resisted their "natural" roles.
author: Sigmund Freud

text: He had a sharp vision; no illusions lulled him to sleep except for an often exaggerated faith in his own ideas.
author: Sigmund Freud
source: Albert Einstein , as quoted in Sigmund Freud (2006) by Kathleen Krull and Boris Kulikov, p. 132

text: Had Freud not discovered psychotherapy, then someone else would have.
author: Sigmund Freud
source: Peter Farb , Man's Rise to Civilization (1968)

text: Society has to control desires, or there would be total anarchy. Yet, everybody has the same desires.
author: Sigmund Freud
source: Rosario Ferré interview in Backtalk: Women Writers Speak Out by Donna Marie Perry (1993)

text: Freudianism has become, with its confessionals and penance, its proselytes and converts, our modern Church. For those who persist in skepticism, there is always that dreadful word 'resistance': they are the sickest, for they fight it so much.
author: Sigmund Freud
source: Shulamith Firestone , The Dialectic of Sex : The Case for Feminist Revolution . 1970. p. 42.

text: Freud captured the imagination of a whole continent and civilization because he grasped the crucial problem of modern life: Sexuality.
author: Sigmund Freud
source: Shulamith Firestone , The Dialectic of Sex : The Case for Feminist Revolution . 1970. p. 43.

text: Freud was merely a diagnostician for what feminism purports to cure.
author: Sigmund Freud
source: Shulamith Firestone , The Dialectic of Sex : The Case for Feminist Revolution . 1970. pp. 43-44.

text: His failure to question society itself was responsible for massive confusion, resulting from the basic contradiction of trying to resolve a problem within the environment that created it.
author: Sigmund Freud
source: Shulamith Firestone , The Dialectic of Sex : The Case for Feminist Revolution . 1970. p. 46.

text: I believe Freud was talking about something real, though perhaps his ideas, taken literally, lead to absurdity – for his genius was poetic rather than scientific; his ideas are more valuable as metaphors than as literal truths.
author: Sigmund Freud
source: Shulamith Firestone , The Dialectic of Sex : The Case for Feminist Revolution . 1970. p. 46.

text: If the evolution of civilization has such a far-reaching similarity with the development of an individual, would not the diagnosis be justified that the whole of humanity has become 'neurotic' under the pressure of civilizing trends?
author: Sigmund Freud

text: Freud was one of the last representatives of Enlightenment philosophy. He genuinely believed in reason as the one strength man has and which alone could save him from confusion and decay.
author: Sigmund Freud
source: Erich Fromm , in The Anatomy of Human Destructiveness (1977)

text: While the implications of Darwin’s views were threatening and unsettling, they were not quite so directly abrasive, not quite so unrespectable, as Freud’s views on infantile sexuality, the ubiquity of perversions, and the dynamic power of unconscious urges.
author: Sigmund Freud
source: Peter Gay (1987). A Godless Jew: Freud, Atheism, and the Making of Psychoanalysis . New Haven, CT: Yale University Press, p. 144

text: Darwin trusted the passage of time and the weight of his argumentation, while Freud orchestrated his wooing of the public mind through a loyal cadre of adherents.
author: Sigmund Freud
source: Peter Gay (1987). A Godless Jew: Freud, Atheism, and the Making of Psychoanalysis . New Haven, CT: Yale University Press, p. 145

text: Freud's simplicity, earnestness, and brilliance led one out of a dark cellar into broad daylight. For the first time, I grasped the full significance of sex repression and its effect on human thought and action, and understood myself.
author: Sigmund Freud

text: The most important scientific revolutions all include, as their only common feature, the dethronement of human arrogance from one pedestal after another of previous convictions about our centrality in the cosmos.
author: Sigmund Freud
source: As mentioned by Stephen Jay Gould, in the essay collection book: "Dinosaur in a Haystack: Reflections in Natural History, Part Three: 'Origin, Stability, And Extinction', Chapter 13: 'Jove's Thunderbolts', p. 164-165 - Three Rivers Press. New York. 1996 -- ISBN-10: 0517888246 ISBN-13: 978-0517888247 (original edition) -- Available: Belknap Press; Reprint edition (2011) -- ISBN-10: 0674061608 ISBN-13: 978-0674061606 (reprint)

text: According to Freud, our best and highest aspirations are merely symptoms of neurosis. He defines genius as nothing more than sublimated sexual drives, and our subconscious as a sewer inhabited by monsters and vile incestuous desires.
author: Sigmund Freud
source: Nina Graboi One Foot in the Future: A Woman's Spiritual Journey (2000), Chapter Twenty-three

text: I am fascinated by the fact that thousands of people continue to idealize and defend [Freud] without really knowing anything about him as a person.
author: Sigmund Freud
source: Phyllis Grosskurth (1991). The Secret Ring: Freud’s Inner Circle and the Politics of Psychoanalysis . Boston: Addison-Wesley, p. 219

text: Kierkegaard and Freud, though they never knew each other, shared a lifelong preoccupation with anxiety. Their elucidation and treatment of this problem, despite working independently, leads to surprising results: they confirm each other in their conclusions, criticize each other in their limitations, and match each other perfectly.
author: Sigmund Freud
source: Freud And The 20th Century 1958 Edited by Benjamin Nelson ISBN10 0548443815

text: Most dreams are neither obscure nor bowdlerized, but rather transparent and unedited, revealing clearly meaningful, undisguised, and often highly conflictual themes.
author: Sigmund Freud
source: J. Allan Hobson , in The Dreaming Brain : How the brain creates both the sense and nonsense of dreams (1988)

text: Your technique of treating your pupils like patients is a blunder. In that way you produce either slavish sons or impudent puppies...
author: Sigmund Freud

text: The Freudian revolution revealed that we do not consciously control our own actions but are instead driven by unconscious motives, and that human creativity stems from conscious access to these underlying forces.
author: Sigmund Freud
source: Eric Kandel , The Age of Insight (2012)

text: One of the most important ways of understanding the unconscious—indeed, as Freud saw it, the royal road to discovering the nature of its contents—is the dream.
author: Sigmund Freud
source: Morton Kelsey , Myth, History & Faith: The Mysteries of Christian Myth & Imagination (1974) Ch.VII

text: From a scientific point of view, classical Freudian psychoanalysis is dead as both a theory of the mind and a mode of therapy. No empirical evidence supports any specific proposition of psychoanalytic theory. Freud is better studied as a writer, in departments of language and literature, than as a scientist, in departments of psychology.
author: Sigmund Freud
source: John F. Kihlstrom, quoted in Antonio de Nicolas, Krishnan Ramaswamy, and Aditi Banerjee (eds.) (2007), Invading the Sacred: An Analysis Of Hinduism Studies In America (Publisher: Rupa & Co., p. 273ff) John F. Kihlstrom, “Is Freud Still Alive? No. Not Really.”

text: Whatever you call it, there is a struggle in the universe between good and evil. Not only is that struggle structured in the external forces of the universe, it's structured in our own lives.
author: Sigmund Freud
source: 1968 writing included in The Autobiography of Martin Luther King, Jr. (1998)

text: The basic assumption of Freud is that none of us is responsible for what we are, but merely victims of our past. This grossly simplistic idea has dominated the thinking of our century.
author: Sigmund Freud
source: Dean Koontz , as quoted in Nick Gillespie & Lisa Snell, Contemplating Evil: Novelist Dean Koontz on Freud, fraud, and the Great Society , Reason magazine, 1996

text: Every time I see a photograph of Freud I wonder how a man who spent his whole life tête-à-tête with sex can look that gloomy.
author: Sigmund Freud
source: Raymond Loewy , in Never Leave Well Enough Alone (1951)

text: For Freud the ultimate psychological reality is the system of attractions and tensions which attaches the child to parental images, and then through these to all other persons.
author: Sigmund Freud
source: Maurice Merleau-Ponty , as quoted in The Essential Writings of Merleau-Ponty (1969) edited by A. L. Fisher

text: The risk is not that Freudian research will shock us by recalling the 'barbarian' in us, but that its findings will be too easily accepted in an 'idealist' form.
author: Sigmund Freud
source: Maurice Merleau-Ponty , as quoted in The Essential Writings of Merleau-Ponty (1969) edited by A. L. Fisher

text: An expert is someone who rarely slips up—because of knowing what not to do.
author: Sigmund Freud

text: Freud is all nonsense; the secret of neurosis is to be found in the family battle of wills to see who can refuse the longest to help with the dishes.
author: Sigmund Freud
source: Julian Mitchell , in As Far as You Can Go (1963), Pt. 1, Ch. 1

text: Whereas Freud was for the most part concerned with the morbid effects of unconscious repression, Jung was more interested in the manifestations of unconscious expression, first in the dream and eventually in all the more orderly products of religion and art and morals.
author: Sigmund Freud
source: Lewis Mumford in Interpretations and Forecasts (1967)

text: I am myself the very subject of my book.
author: Michel de Montaigne
source: I want to be seen here in my simple, natural, ordinary fashion, without straining or artifice; for it is myself that I portray...I am myself the matter of my book.

text: Man is a wonderfully vain, diverse, and wavering subject. It is difficult to found a constant and uniform judgment upon him.
author: Michel de Montaigne
source: Truly man is a marvellously vain, diverse, and undulating object. It is hard to found any constant and uniform judgement on him.

text: All passions that suffer themselves to be relished and digested are but moderate.
author: Michel de Montaigne
source: Ch. 2. Of Sorrow (tr. Cotton, rev. W. Hazlitt, 1842)

text: A strong memory is commonly coupled with infirm judgment.
author: Michel de Montaigne
source: Ch. 9. Of Liars (tr. Cotton, rev. W. Carew Hazlitt, 1877)

text: It is not without good reason said, that he who has not a good memory should never take upon him the trade of lying.
author: Michel de Montaigne
source: Ch. 9. Of Liars (tr. Cotton, rev. W. Hazlitt, 1842)

text: For the extraordinary, all the provision in the world could not suffice.
author: Michel de Montaigne

text: Many flee tranquil lives for the horror of deserts, embracing humiliation and contempt, even seeking them out.
author: Michel de Montaigne

text: Things are not so painful and difficult of themselves, but our weakness or cowardice makes them so.
author: Michel de Montaigne
source: Ch. 14 (tr. Cotton, rev. W. Carew Hazlitt, 1877)

text: We are double in ourselves, believing what we do not believe, and unable to disengage from what we condemn.
author: Michel de Montaigne
source: Ch. 16. Of Glory (tr. Cotton, rev. W. Carew Hazlitt, 1877)

text: The thing I fear most is fear itself.
author: Michel de Montaigne
source: The thing I fear most is fear .

text: He who should teach men to die would at the same time teach them to live.
author: Michel de Montaigne
source: Ch. 18. That Men are not to judge of our Happiness till after Death (tr. Cotton, rev. W. Hazlitt, 1842)

text: I want death to find me planting my cabbages.
author: Michel de Montaigne
source: I want death to find me planting my cabbages.

text: All the opinions of the world agree in this, that pleasure is our end.
author: Michel de Montaigne
source: Ch. 20. Of the Force of Imagination (tr. Cotton, rev. W. Carew Hazlitt, 1877)

text: He who would teach men to die would teach them to live.
author: Michel de Montaigne
source: Ch. 20. Of the Force of Imagination (tr. Donald M. Frame)

text: The day of your birth is one day’s advance towards the grave.
author: Michel de Montaigne
source: Ch. 20. Of the Force of Imagination (tr. Cotton, rev. W. Carew Hazlitt, 1877) Cf. Dávid Baróti Szabó , Nem kímíl meg senkit halál (wr. 1786; ed. 1914)

text: Live as long as you please, you will strike nothing off the time you will have to spend dead.
author: Michel de Montaigne
source: Ch. 20. Of the Force of Imagination

text: The utility of living consists not in the length of days, but in the use of time; a man may have lived long, and yet lived but a little.
author: Michel de Montaigne

text: All of the days go toward death and the last one arrives there.
author: Michel de Montaigne
source: Ch. 20. Of the Force of Imagination

text: The laws of conscience, which we pretend to be derived from nature, proceed from custom.
author: Michel de Montaigne
source: Ch. 22. Of Custom (tr. Cotton, rev. W. Hazlitt, 1842)

text: We must not attach knowledge to the mind, we have to incorporate it there.
author: Michel de Montaigne

text: Every other knowledge is harmful to him who does not have knowledge of goodness.
author: Michel de Montaigne

text: Better to prepare with fine assurance for the worst, and find consolation in its uncertainty.
author: Michel de Montaigne
