text: I speak of others only to reveal more of myself.
author: Michel de Montaigne
source: I do not speak the minds of others except to speak my own mind better.

text: Choose a guide with a well-made rather than a well-filled head.
author: Michel de Montaigne
source: Ch. 26. On the Education of Children

text: Accustom him to everything, that he may be a sinewy, hardy, and vigorous young man.
author: Michel de Montaigne
source: Ch. 26. Of the Education of Children (tr. Cotton, rev. W. Hazlitt, 1842)

text: How many things served us yesterday as articles of faith, which are fables to us today?
author: Michel de Montaigne
source: How many things served us yesterday for articles of faith , which today are fables for us?

text: We were halves throughout, and to that degree that, methinks, by outliving him I defraud him of his part.
author: Michel de Montaigne
source: Ch. 27. Of Friendship (tr. Cotton, rev. W. Hazlitt, 1842)

text: If I am pressed to say why I loved him, I feel that it can only be expressed by replying: 'Because it was he; because it was I.'
author: Michel de Montaigne
source: If you press me to say why I loved him, I can say no more than it was because he was he, and I was I.

text: There are some defeats more triumphant than victories.
author: Michel de Montaigne
source: Ch. 30. Of Cannibals (tr. Cotton, rev. W. Hazlitt, 1842)

text: Nothing is believed so firmly as what is least known.
author: Michel de Montaigne
source: Nothing is so firmly believed as what we least know.

text: A wise man never loses anything, if he has himself.
author: Michel de Montaigne
source: Ch. 38. Of Solitude (tr. Cotton, rev. W. Hazlitt, 1842)

text: The man of understanding has lost nothing, if he has himself.
author: Michel de Montaigne
source: A man of understanding has lost nothing, if he has himself.

text: The greatest thing in the world is to know how to belong to oneself.
author: Michel de Montaigne
source: The greatest thing in the world is to know how to belong to oneself.

text: Even opinion is of force enough to make itself to be espoused at the expense of life.
author: Michel de Montaigne
source: Book I, Ch. 40. Of Good and Evil (tr. Cotton, rev. W. Hazlitt, 1842)

text: He who does not give himself leisure to be thirsty cannot take pleasure in drinking.
author: Michel de Montaigne

text: Kings and philosophers defecate, and ladies too.
author: Michel de Montaigne
source: Kings and philosophers shit, and so do ladies. Ch. 42, English translation from Hartle, Ann (2003), Michel de Montaigne: Accidental Philosopher , Cambridge University Press.

text: God's justice and His power are inseparable; it is in vain we invoke His power in an unjust cause. We must have our souls pure and clean, purified from all vicious passions, when we pray to Him.
author: Michel de Montaigne
source: Ch. 56. Of Prayers (tr. Cotton, rev. W. Carew Hazlitt, 1877)

text: A true prayer cannot enter an impure soul. He who calls God to his assistance whilst in a course of vice, does as if a cut-purse should call a magistrate to help him.
author: Michel de Montaigne
source: Ch. 56 (tr. Cotton, rev. W. Carew Hazlitt, 1877)

text: There is nothing so easy, so sweet, and so favourable, as the divine law: it calls and invites us to her, guilty and abominable as we are; extends her arms and receives us into her bosom. But in return, we are to receive this pardon with gratitude and submission, and for that instant, have the soul sensible of the ills we have committed, and at enmity with those passions that seduced us.
author: Michel de Montaigne
source: Ch. 56 (tr. Cotton, rev. W. Carew Hazlitt, 1877)

text: There is as much difference between us and ourselves as between us and others.
author: Michel de Montaigne
source: Ch. 1. Of the Inconstancy of Our Actions (tr. Cotton, rev. W. Carew Hazlitt, 1877)

text: It is the part of cowardice, not of courage, to go and crouch in a hole under a massive tomb, to avoid the blows of fortune.
author: Michel de Montaigne
source: Ch. 3. A Usage of the Island of Cea (tr. George B. Ives, 1925)

text: It is a thorny enterprise, and more than it seems, to follow the vagabond course of our mind; to penetrate the opaque depths of its internal folds; to choose and arrest its minute agitations.
author: Michel de Montaigne
source: It is a thorny undertaking, and more so than it seems, to follow a movement so wandering as that of our mind, to penetrate the opaque depths of its innermost folds, to pick out and immobilize the innumerable flutterings that agitate it.

text: It is folly and injustice to deprive children, when grown up, of familiarity with their father, and to carry a scornful and austere countenance toward them, thinking by that to keep them in awe and obedience; for it renders fathers distasteful, and, which is worse, ridiculous to their own children.
author: Michel de Montaigne
source: Ch. 8. On the Affections of Fathers to their Children (tr. Cotton, rev. W. Carew Hazlitt, 1877)

text: Virtue refuses facility for her companion. The easy, gentle path is not the path of true virtue; it demands a rough and thorny road.
author: Michel de Montaigne
source: Ch. 11. Of Cruelty (tr. Donald M. Frame)

text: For my own part, I cannot without grief see so much as an innocent beast pursued and killed that has no defence, and from which we have received no offence at all.
author: Michel de Montaigne

text: When I play with my cat, who knows whether she is not passing her time with me, more than I with her.
author: Michel de Montaigne
source: When I play with my cat , who knows if I am not a pastime to her more than she is to me?

text: All that is under heaven runs one law and one fortune.
author: Michel de Montaigne
source: Ch. 12 (tr. Cotton, rev. W. Carew Hazlitt, 1877)

text: As to fidelity, there is no animal in the world so treacherous as man.
author: Michel de Montaigne
source: Ch. 12 (tr. Cotton, rev. W. Carew Hazlitt, 1877)

text: The souls of emperors and cobblers are cast in the same mold...The same reason that makes us wrangle with a neighbor creates a war betwixt princes.
author: Michel de Montaigne
source: Ch. 12 (tr. Cotton, rev. W. Carew Hazlitt, 1877)

text: The plague of man is boasting of his knowledge.
author: Michel de Montaigne

text: The first law God gave to man was pure obedience, a commandment naked and simple, for to obey is the proper office of a rational soul acknowledging a heavenly superior.
author: Michel de Montaigne

text: Our faith is not of our own acquiring; it is purely the gift of another's bounty. It is more by the mediation of our ignorance than of our knowledge that we know anything of divine wisdom. For God has chosen the simple and ignorant to instruct us, and as it is written, 'I will destroy the wisdom of the wise, and bring to nothing the understanding of the prudent.'
author: Michel de Montaigne

text: Of all opinions concerning religion, the most excusable acknowledges God as an incomprehensible power, the original and preserver of all things, all goodness, all perfection, receiving man's honour and reverence under whatever method or name.
author: Michel de Montaigne

text: Man is forming thousands of ridiculous relations between himself and God.
author: Michel de Montaigne

text: Atheism, however arrogant, is difficult to establish in the human understanding. Men profess it out of vanity and pride, yet will lift their hands to heaven if thrust with a sword, and when fear or sickness abates their giddy humour, they easily reconcile to public faith.
author: Michel de Montaigne

text: To an atheist all writings tend to atheism: he corrupts the most innocent matter with his own venom.
author: Michel de Montaigne

text: Man is truly foolish. He cannot create a single mite, yet he forges gods by the dozen.
author: Michel de Montaigne
source: Man is certainly crazy. He could not make a mite, and he makes gods by the dozen.

text: What truth do these mountains confine, that becomes a falsehood beyond?
author: Michel de Montaigne
source: What of a truth that is bounded by these mountains and is falsehood to the world that lives beyond?

text: Those who likened our life to a dream were wise. We wake while sleeping, and sleep while waking.
author: Michel de Montaigne
source: Those who have compared our life to a dream were right. ... We sleeping wake, and waking asleep.

text: When you see a stately edifice, you conclude it was not built for rats. Have we not reason to believe this divine structure of the celestial palace is the residence of a possessor much greater than we?
author: Michel de Montaigne
source: Ch. 12 (tr. Cotton, rev. W. Carew Hazlitt, 1877)

text: We are no nearer heaven on the top of Mount Cenis than at the bottom of the sea.
author: Michel de Montaigne

text: We are beholden to God only, and to the favour of his grace, for the truth of so noble a belief, since from his sole bounty we receive the fruit of immortality, which consists in the enjoyment of eternal beatitude.
author: Michel de Montaigne

text: God might grant us riches, honours, life, and even health, to our own hurt; for everything pleasing to us is not always good. If He sends us death or sickness, 'Thy rod and thy staff have comforted me,' for He does it by the rule of His providence, which better discerns what is proper for us.
author: Michel de Montaigne

text: All the abuses of the world are begotten by our being taught to be afraid of professing our ignorance, and that we are bound to accept all things we are not able to refute. They make me hate things that are likely, when they would impose them upon me as infallible.
author: Michel de Montaigne
source: Ch. 12 (tr. Cotton, rev. W. Carew Hazlitt, 1877)

text: God, who is all fulness and perfection, cannot augment Himself; but His name may be increased by the praise we attribute to His works. To God alone glory and honour appertain; for, being imperfect and continually needing amelioration, it is to that we ought to employ all our endeavour.
author: Michel de Montaigne

text: How many valiant men we have seen to survive their own reputation!
author: Michel de Montaigne

text: I find that the best goodness I have has some tincture of vice.
author: Michel de Montaigne

text: Saying is one thing and doing is another.
author: Michel de Montaigne

text: As far as physicians go, chance is more valuable than knowledge.
author: Michel de Montaigne

text: Physicians have this advantage: the sun lights their success and the earth covers their failures.
author: Michel de Montaigne

text: There were never in the world two opinions alike, any more than two hairs or two grains. Their most universal quality is diversity.
author: Michel de Montaigne

text: I will follow the good side right to the fire, but not into it if I can help it.
author: Michel de Montaigne

text: I speak the truth, not my fill of it, but as much as I dare speak; and I dare to do so a little more as I grow old.
author: Michel de Montaigne

text: Few men have been admired by their own households.
author: Michel de Montaigne

text: Each man bears the full imprint of the human condition.
author: Michel de Montaigne
source: Every man bears the whole stamp of the human condition.

text: I may desire to be other than I am, but repentance does not properly touch things that are not in our power. I cannot improve my faculties simply by conceiving of others more elevated than mine.
author: Michel de Montaigne

text: Malice sucks up the greatest part of its own venom, and poisons itself.
author: Michel de Montaigne

text: Let no man be ashamed to speak what he is not ashamed to think.
author: Michel de Montaigne

text: It happens as with cages: the birds without despair to get in, and those within despair of getting out.
author: Michel de Montaigne

text: I look upon all men as my compatriots, embracing a Pole as a Frenchman, making less account of the national than of the universal and common bond.
author: Michel de Montaigne

text: There is no man so good that, if all his actions and thoughts were put to the test of the law, he would not be hanged ten times in his life.
author: Michel de Montaigne
source: There is no man so good that if he placed all his actions and thoughts under the scrutiny of the laws , he would not deserve hanging ten times in his life.

text: A man must be a little mad if he does not want to be even more stupid.
author: Michel de Montaigne

text: At the beginning of my sicknesses, I reconcile myself to Almighty God by the last Christian offices, and find myself by so doing less oppressed and more easy, having gained so much the better of my disease.
author: Michel de Montaigne

text: Lend yourself to others, but give yourself to yourself.
author: Michel de Montaigne

text: I have seen no more evident monstrosity and miracle in the world than myself.
author: Michel de Montaigne

text: I have only gathered here a bouquet of foreign flowers, providing nothing of my own but the thread to bind them.
author: Michel de Montaigne
source: I have gathered a posy of other men’s flowers , and nothing but the thread that binds them is mine own.

text: To hope that man should rise above himself and humanity is impossible. He shall be exalted only if God lends him an extraordinary hand, by abandoning his own means and being raised by purely celestial means. This belongs to Christian faith, not stoical virtue.
author: Michel de Montaigne

text: There is no wish more natural than the wish to know.
author: Michel de Montaigne

text: It is more of a job to interpret the interpretations than to interpret the things, and there are more books about books than about any other subject: we do nothing but write glosses about each other.
author: Michel de Montaigne

text: For truth itself does not have the privilege to be employed at any time and in every way; its use, noble as it is, has its circumscriptions and limits.
author: Michel de Montaigne

text: The life of Caesar has no more to show us than our own; an emperor's or an ordinary man's, it is still a life subject to all human accidents.
author: Michel de Montaigne

text: Though we may mount on stilts, we must still walk on our own legs. And on the highest throne in the world, we are still only sitting on our own behind.
author: Michel de Montaigne
source: No matter that we may mount on stilts, we still must walk on our own legs. And on the highest throne in the world, we still sit only on our own bottom.

text: Let us give Nature a chance; she knows her business better than we do.
author: Michel de Montaigne

text: It would be better to have no laws at all than to have them in such profusion as we do.
author: Michel de Montaigne

text: In this present that God has made us, there is nothing unworthy our care; we stand accountable for it even to a hair. It is a commission to man, to conduct man according to his condition, prescribed by the Creator.
author: Michel de Montaigne

text: Plato says, 'Tis to no purpose for a sober man to knock at the door of the Muses;' and Aristotle says 'that no excellent soul is exempt from a mixture of folly.'
author: Michel de Montaigne

text: For a desperate disease a desperate cure.
author: Michel de Montaigne
source: Book II, Ch. 3. The Custom of the Isle of Cea

text: He who confers a benefit on anyone loves him better than he is beloved by him again.
author: Michel de Montaigne
source: Book II, Ch. 8. Of the Affections of Fathers

text: The middle sort of historians spoil all; they will chew our meat for us.
author: Michel de Montaigne

text: Virtue requires a rough and stormy passage; she will have either outward difficulties to wrestle with, or internal difficulties.
author: Michel de Montaigne

text: Our moral progress may be measured by the degree in which we sympathize with individual suffering and individual joy.
author: George Eliot

text: If art does not enlarge men's sympathies, it does nothing morally.
author: George Eliot

text: It is the living only who cannot be forgiven. While the heart beats, bruise it—it is your only opportunity. The heart will by and by be still, where savage indignation can no longer tear the heart.
author: George Eliot
source: The Lifted Veil (1859); Eliot here quotes the Latin epitaph of Jonathan Swift , translated as "Where savage indignation can lacerate his heart no more" · The Lifted Veil online at Wikisource

text: The only failure a man ought to fear is failure of cleaving to the purpose he sees to be best.
author: George Eliot

text: An election is coming. Universal peace is declared, and the foxes have a sincere interest in prolonging the lives of the poultry.
author: George Eliot

text: 'Tis God gives skill, But not without men's hands: He could not make Antonio Stradivari's violins Without Antonio.
author: George Eliot

text: I like not only to be loved, but also to be told that I am loved. The realm of silence is large enough beyond the grave. This is the world of light and speech, and I shall take leave to tell you that you are very dear.
author: George Eliot
source: Letter to Georgiana Burne-Jones , wife of the artist Edward Burne-Jones (1875)

text: Blessed is the man who, having nothing to say, abstains from giving us wordy evidence of the fact.
author: George Eliot
source: Impressions of Theophrastus Such , Ch, 4 (1879); comparable to. James Russell Lowell 1871: Blessed are they who have nothing to say, and who cannot be persuaded to say it.

text: The darkest night that ever fell upon the earth never hid the light, never put out the stars. It only made the stars more keenly, kindly glancing, as if in protest against the darkness.
author: George Eliot
source: As quoted in Golden Gleams of Thought from the Words of Leading Orators, Divines, Philosophers, Statesmen and Poets (1881) by S. Pollock Linn; also in Still Waters (1913)

text: The golden moments in the stream of life rush past us, and we see nothing but sand; the angels come to visit us, and we only know them when they are gone.
author: George Eliot
source: Reported in Josiah Hotchkiss Gilbert, Dictionary of Burning Words of Brilliant Writers (1895), p. 563

text: What do we live for, if it is not to make life less difficult for each other?
author: George Eliot

text: May I unceasingly aspire to unclothe all around me of its conventional, human, temporary dress, to look at it in its essence and in its relation to eternity.
author: George Eliot
source: Letters, ed. Gordon Sherman Haight, vol. 1, p. 170

text: It is so much easier to make up your mind that your neighbour is good for nothing, than to enter into all the circumstances that would oblige you to modify that opinion.
author: George Eliot
source: "The Sad Fortunes of the Rev. Amos Barton" Ch. 4

text: Every man who is not a monster, a mathematician, or a mad philosopher, is the slave of some woman or other.
author: George Eliot
source: "The Sad Fortunes of the Rev. Amos Barton" Ch. 4

text: Depend upon it, you would gain unspeakably if you would learn to see some of the poetry and the pathos, the tragedy and the comedy, lying in the experience of a human soul that looks out through dull grey eyes, and that speaks in a voice of quite ordinary tones.
author: George Eliot
source: "The Sad Fortunes of the Rev. Amos Barton" Ch. 5

text: Any coward can fight a battle when he's sure of winning; but give me the man who has pluck to fight when he's sure of losing. There are many victories worse than a defeat.
author: George Eliot

text: Opposition may become sweet to a man when he has christened it persecution.
author: George Eliot

text: The blessed work of helping the world forward, happily does not wait to be done by perfect men.
author: George Eliot
source: "Janet's Repentance" Ch. 10 in Scenes of Clerical Life (1858); this has appeared in paraphrased form as: " The important work of moving the world forward does not wait to be done by perfect men. "

text: Blessed influence of one true, loving human soul on another. Not calculable by algebra, not deducible by logic, but mysterious, effectual, mighty as the hidden process by which the tiny seed is quickened, and bursts forth into tall stem and broad leaf, and glowing tasselled flower.
author: George Eliot
source: "Janet's Repentance" Ch. 19. Often given as "Blessed is the influence..."

text: Worldly faces, never look so worldly as at a funeral.
author: George Eliot

text: Who can prove Wit to be witty when with deeper ground Dulness intuitive declares wit dull?
author: George Eliot
source: A College Breakfast-party , reported in Bartlett's Familiar Quotations , 10th ed. (1919)

text: Our dead are never dead to us until we have forgotten them.
author: George Eliot

text: It's but little good you'll do a-watering the last year's crop.
author: George Eliot

text: Deep, unspeakable suffering may well be called a baptism, a regeneration, the initiation into a new state.
author: George Eliot

text: We hand folks over to God 's mercy , and show none ourselves.
author: George Eliot

text: Our deeds determine us, as much as we determine our deeds. There is a terrible coercion in our deeds, which may first turn the honest man into a deceiver and then reconcile him to the change, for the second wrong presents itself to him in the guise of the only practicable right.
author: George Eliot

text: Consequences are unpitying. Our deeds carry their terrible consequences, quite apart from any fluctuations that went before — consequences that are hardly ever confined to ourselves.
author: George Eliot

text: Family likeness has often a deep sadness in it. Nature, that great tragic dramatist, knits us together by bone and muscle, and divides us by the subtler web of our brains; blends yearning and repulsion; and ties us by our heart-strings to the beings that jar us at every movement.
author: George Eliot

text: Imagination is a licensed trespasser: it has no fear of dogs, but may climb over walls and peep in at windows with impunity.
author: George Eliot

text: The nature of things doesn't change, though it seems as if one's own life was nothing but change. The best of working is, it gives you a grip hold of things outside your own lot.
author: George Eliot

text: Love has a way of cheating itself consciously, like a child who plays at solitary hide-and-seek; it is pleased with assurances that it all the while disbelieves.
author: George Eliot

text: There are folks who make bad butter and trust to the salt to hide it.
author: George Eliot

text: Destiny disguises her cold awful face behind a hazy radiant veil, encloses us in warm downy wings, and poisons us with violet-scented breath.
author: George Eliot

text: Such young unfurrowed souls roll to meet each other like two velvet peaches that touch softly and are at rest; they mingle as easily as two brooklets that ask for nothing but to entwine themselves and ripple with ever-interlacing curves in the leafiest hiding-places.
author: George Eliot

text: Her heart lived in no cherished secrets of its own, but in feelings which it longed to share with all the world.
author: George Eliot

text: People who love downy peaches are apt not to think of the stone, and sometimes jar their teeth terribly against it.
author: George Eliot

text: No dust has settled on one's mind then, and it presents a clear mirror to the rays of things.
author: George Eliot

text: Falsehood is so easy, truth so difficult. Examine your words well, and you will find that even when you have no motive to be false, it is a very hard thing to say the exact truth, even about your own immediate feelings — much harder than to say something fine about them which is not the exact truth.
author: George Eliot

text: Human feeling is like the mighty rivers that bless the earth: it does not wait for beauty — it flows with resistless force and brings beauty with it.
author: George Eliot

text: Let us love that beauty which lies in no secret of proportion, but in the secret of deep human sympathy. I can't afford to give all my love and reverence to rarities: I want a great deal of those feelings for my every-day fellow-men.
author: George Eliot

text: Perhaps nothing would be a lesson to us if it didn't come too late.
author: George Eliot

text: A man never lies with more delicious languor under the influence of a passion than when he has persuaded himself that he shall subdue it to-morrow.
author: George Eliot

text: There are so many of us, and our lots are so different, what wonder that Nature's mood is often in harsh contrast with the great crisis of our lives? We must learn not to expect that our hurts will be made much of, but to help each other the more.
author: George Eliot

text: There is no despair so absolute as that which comes with the first moments of our first great sorrow, when we have not yet known what it is to have suffered and be healed, to have despaired and to have recovered hope.
author: George Eliot

text: There's no pleasure in living if you're to be corked up forever, and only dribble your mind out by the sly, like a leaky barrel.
author: George Eliot

text: It is well known to all experienced minds that our firmest convictions are often dependent on subtle impressions for which words are quite too coarse a medium.
author: George Eliot

text: Men's lives are as thoroughly blended with each other as the air they breathe: evil spreads as necessarily as disease.
author: George Eliot

text: Doubtless a great anguish may do the work of years, and we may come out from that baptism of fire with a soul full of new awe and new pity.
author: George Eliot

text: How is it that poets speak so much of first love, and so little of later love? Are not those the best poems which come from fuller thought, larger experience, and deeper-rooted affections?
author: George Eliot

text: What greater thing is there for two human souls, than to feel that they are joined for life — to strengthen each other in all labour, to rest on each other in all sorrow, to minister to each other in all pain, to be one with each other in silent unspeakable memories at the moment of the last parting?
author: George Eliot

text: There's a sort of wrong that can never be made up for.
author: George Eliot

text: He was like a cock who thought the sun had risen to hear him crow.
author: George Eliot
source: Chapter 33. Compare: Edmond Rostand , Chantecler: Hymn to the Sun , Act II, Sc. 3: Je recule Ébloui de me voir moi même tout vermeil Et d’avoir, moi, le coq, fait élever le soleil. I fall back dazzled at beholding myself all rosy red, At having, I myself, caused the sun to rise.

text: However, I'm not denying women are foolish: God Almighty made them to match the men.
author: George Eliot

text: Anger and jealousy can no more bear to lose sight of their objects than love...
author: George Eliot

text: Our life is determined for us — and it makes the mind very free when we give up wishing and only think of bearing what is laid upon us and doing what is given us to do.
author: George Eliot

text: The happiest women, like the happiest nations, have no history.
author: George Eliot

text: I should like to know what is the proper function of women, if it is not to make reasons for husbands to stay at home, and still stronger reasons for bachelors to go out.
author: George Eliot

text: Music seems to infuse strength into my limbs, and ideas into my brain. Life seems to go on without effort, when I am filled with music.
author: George Eliot

text: There is no feeling, except the extremes of fear and grief, that does not find relief in music.
author: George Eliot

text: I've never any pity for conceited people, because I think they carry their comfort about with them.
author: George Eliot

text: Childhood has no forebodings; but then, it is soothed by no memories of outlived sorrow.
author: George Eliot

text: Better spend an extra hundred or two on your son's education, than leave it him in your will.
author: George Eliot

text: The bitter sorrows of childhood, when sorrow is all new and strange, when hope has not yet got wings to fly beyond the days and weeks, and the space from summer to summer seems measureless.
author: George Eliot

text: We could never have loved the earth so well if we had had no childhood in it...
author: George Eliot

text: If a man means to be hard, let him keep in his saddle and speak from that height, above the level of pleading eyes, and with the command of a distant horizon.
author: George Eliot

text: Ugly and deformed people have great need of unusual virtues, because they are likely to be extremely uncomfortable without them.
author: George Eliot

text: High achievements demand some other unusual qualification besides an unusual desire for high prizes.
author: George Eliot

text: It is doubtful whether our soldiers would be maintained if there were not pacific people at home who like to fancy themselves soldiers. War, like other dramatic spectacles, might possibly cease for want of a "public."
author: George Eliot

text: If boys and men are to be welded together in the glow of transient feeling, they must be made of metal that will mix, else they inevitably fall asunder when the heat dies out.
author: George Eliot

text: If you want to slip into a round hole, you must make a ball of yourself.
author: George Eliot

text: It seems to me we can never give up longing and wishing while we are thoroughly alive. There are certain things we feel to be beautiful and good, and we must hunger after them. How can we ever be satisfied without them until our feelings are deadened?
author: George Eliot

text: She and Stephen were in that stage of courtship which makes the most exquisite moment of youth, the freshest blossom-time of passion, — when each is sure of the other's love, but no formal declaration has been made, and all is mutual divination, exalting the most trivial word, the lightest gesture, into thrills delicate and delicious as wafted jasmine scent.
author: George Eliot

text: There is something strangely winning to most women in that offer of the firm arm; the help is not wanted physically at that moment, but the sense of help, the presence of strength that is outside them and yet theirs, meets a continual want of the imagination.
author: George Eliot

text: Jealousy is never satisfied with anything short of an omniscience that would detect the subtlest fold of the heart.
author: George Eliot

text: More helpful than all wisdom is one draught of simple human pity that will not forsake us.
author: George Eliot

text: Nature repairs her ravages, but not all. The uptorn trees are not rooted again; the parted hills are left scarred; if there is a new growth, the trees are not the same as the old, and the hills underneath their green vesture bear the marks of the past rending. To the eyes that have dwelt on the past, there is no thorough repair.
author: George Eliot

text: Renunciation remains sorrow, though a sorrow borne willingly.
author: George Eliot

text: The need of being loved, the strongest need, began to wrestle with her pride and soon threw it.
author: George Eliot

text: Every man's work, pursued steadily, tends in this way to become an end in itself, and so to bridge over the loveless chasms of his life.
author: George Eliot
source: Chapter 2 (at page 16 – Page numbers as per the 1996 Penguin Classics Edition)
source_section: Silas Marner: The Weaver of Raveloe (1861)

text: He hated the thought of the past; there was nothing that called out his love and fellowship toward the strangers he had come amongst; and the future was all dark.
author: George Eliot
source_section: Silas Marner: The Weaver of Raveloe (1861)

text: Do we not wile away moments of inanity or fatigued waiting by repeating some trivial movement or sound, until the repetition has bred a want, which is incipient habit?
author: George Eliot
source_section: Silas Marner: The Weaver of Raveloe (1861)

text: The rich ate and drank freely, accepting gout and apoplexy as things that ran mysteriously in respectable families.
author: George Eliot
source_section: Silas Marner: The Weaver of Raveloe (1861)

text: That big muscular frame of his held plenty of animal courage, but helped him to no decision when the dangers to be braved were such as could neither be knocked down nor throttled.
author: George Eliot
source_section: Silas Marner: The Weaver of Raveloe (1861)

text: The yoke a man creates for himself by wrong-doing will breed hate in the kindliest nature.
author: George Eliot
source_section: Silas Marner: The Weaver of Raveloe (1861)

text: The lapse of time during which a given event has not happened, is, in this logic of habit, constantly alleged as a reason why the event should never happen, even when the lapse of time is precisely the added condition which makes the event imminent.
author: George Eliot
source_section: Silas Marner: The Weaver of Raveloe (1861)

text: There are always two opinions: the opinion a man has of himself, and the opinion other people have of him. There would be two opinions about a cracked bell, if the bell could hear itself.
author: George Eliot
source_section: Silas Marner: The Weaver of Raveloe (1861)

text: We cling to the superstitious impression that if we expect evil very strongly it is the less likely to come.
author: George Eliot
source_section: Silas Marner: The Weaver of Raveloe (1861)

text: No sort of duplicity can long flourish without the help of vocal falsehoods.
author: George Eliot
source_section: Silas Marner: The Weaver of Raveloe (1861)

text: Favourable Chance is the god of all men who follow their own devices instead of obeying a law they believe in. The evil principle deprecated in that religion, is the orderly sequence by which the seed brings forth a crop after its kind.
author: George Eliot
source_section: Silas Marner: The Weaver of Raveloe (1861)

text: One reason why we are seldom able to comfort our neighbours with our words is that our goodwill gets adulterated, in spite of ourselves, before it can pass our lips. Language is a stream that is almost sure to smack of a mingled soil.
author: George Eliot
source_section: Silas Marner: The Weaver of Raveloe (1861)

text: Kindness fell on him as sunshine falls on the wretched — he had no heart to taste it, and felt that it was very far off him.
author: George Eliot
source_section: Silas Marner: The Weaver of Raveloe (1861)

text: Formerly, his heart had been as a locked casket with its treasure inside; but now the casket was empty, and the lock was broken. Left groping in darkness, with his prop utterly gone, he had a dull and half-despairing sense that if any help came to him it must come from without, a faint consciousness of dependence on their goodwill.
author: George Eliot
source_section: Silas Marner: The Weaver of Raveloe (1861)

text: It is seldom that the miserable can help regarding their misery as a wrong inflicted by those who are less miserable.
author: George Eliot
source_section: Silas Marner: The Weaver of Raveloe (1861)

text: That wide-gazing calm which makes us older human beings, with our inward turmoil, feel a certain awe in the presence of a little child, such as we feel before some quiet majesty or beauty in the earth or sky.
author: George Eliot
source_section: Silas Marner: The Weaver of Raveloe (1861)

text: It's like the night and the morning, and the sleeping and the waking, and the rain and the harvest — one goes and the other comes, and we know nothing how nor where. We may strive and scrat and fend, but it's little we can do after all — the big things come and go with no striving of our own.
author: George Eliot
source_section: Silas Marner: The Weaver of Raveloe (1861)

text: In old days there were angels who came and took men by the hand and led them away from the city of destruction. We see no white-winged angels now. But yet men are led away from threatening destruction: a hand is put into theirs, which leads them forth gently towards a calm and bright land, so that they look no more backward; and the hand may be a little child's.
author: George Eliot
source_section: Silas Marner: The Weaver of Raveloe (1861)

text: That quiet mutual gaze of a trusting husband and wife is like the first moment of rest or refuge from a great weariness or a great danger — not to be interfered with by speech or action which would distract the sensations from the fresh enjoyment of repose.
author: George Eliot
source_section: Silas Marner: The Weaver of Raveloe (1861)

text: That awe of the Divine Nemesis which was felt by religious pagans, and, though it took a more positive form under Christianity, is still felt by the mass of mankind simply as a vague fear at anything which is called wrong-doing. Such terror of the unseen is so far above mere sensual cowardice that it will annihilate that cowardice: it is the initial recognition of a moral law restraining desire, and checks the hard bold scrutiny of imperfect thought into obligations which can never be proved to have any sanctity in the absence of feeling.
author: George Eliot

text: Our deeds are like children that are born to us; they live and act apart from our own will. Nay, children may be strangled, but deeds never: they have an indestructible life both in and out of our consciousness.
author: George Eliot

text: We prepare ourselves for sudden deeds by the reiterated choice of good or evil that gradually determines character.
author: George Eliot

text: And how much better to die in all the happy period of undisillusioned youth, to go out in a blaze of light, than to have your body worn out and old and illusions shattered.
author: Ernest Hemingway
source: Letter to his family (18 October 1918); published in Ernest Hemingway: Selected Letters 1917–1961 (1981) edited by Carlos Baker. It was also published in The Oak Parker (Oak Park, IL) on 16 November 1918. Only 19 years old at the time, Hemingway was recovering from wounds suffered at the front line while serving as a Red Cross volunteer.

text: A man's got to take a lot of punishment to write a really funny book.
author: Ernest Hemingway
source: Letter (6 December 1924); published in Ernest Hemingway: Selected Letters 1917–1961 (1981) edited by Carlos Baker

text: The age demanded that we dance And jammed us into iron pants. And in the end the age was handed The sort of shit that it demanded.
author: Ernest Hemingway
source: "The Age Demanded" in Der Querschnitt (February 1925); as quoted in Sylvia Beach and the Lost Generation (1983) by Noel Riley Fitch

text: You ought to be able to show that you can do it a good deal better than anyone else with the regular tools before you have a license to bring in your own improvements.
author: Ernest Hemingway
source: Letter (15 May 1925); published in Ernest Hemingway: Selected Letters 1917–1961 (1981) edited by Carlos Baker

text: God knows, people who are paid to have attitudes toward things, professional critics, make me sick; camp-following eunuchs of literature. They won't even whore. They're all virtuous and sterile. And how well meaning and high minded. But they're all camp-followers.
author: Ernest Hemingway
source: Letter to Sherwood Anderson (23 May 1925); published in Ernest Hemingway: Selected Letters 1917–1961 (1981) edited by Carlos Baker

text: I wonder what your idea of heaven would be — A beautiful vacuum filled with wealthy monogamists. All powerful and members of the best families all drinking themselves to death. And hell would probably be an ugly vacuum full of poor polygamists unable to obtain booze or with chronic stomach disorders that they called secret sorrows.
author: Ernest Hemingway
source: Letter to F. Scott Fitzgerald (1 July 1925); published in Ernest Hemingway: Selected Letters 1917–1961 (1981) edited by Carlos Baker

text: Writing letters is such a swell way to keep from working and yet feel you've done something.
author: Ernest Hemingway
source: Letter to F. Scott Fitzgerald (1 July 1925); published in Ernest Hemingway: Selected Letters 1917–1961 (1981) edited by Carlos Baker

text: I've tried to reduce profanity but I reduced so much profanity when writing the book that I'm afraid not much could come out. Perhaps we will have to consider it simply as a profane book and hope that the next book will be less profane or perhaps more sacred.
author: Ernest Hemingway
source: About his book, The Sun Also Rises in a letter (21 August 1926); published in Ernest Hemingway: Selected Letters 1917–1961 (1981) edited by Carlos Baker

text: In the fall the war was always there but we did not go to it any more.
author: Ernest Hemingway
source: "In Another Country" in Men Without Women (1927).

text: The good parts of a book may be only something a writer is lucky enough to overhear or it may be the wreck of his whole damn life — and one is as good as the other.
author: Ernest Hemingway
source: Letter to F. Scott Fitzgerald (4 September 1929); published in Ernest Hemingway: Selected Letters 1917–1961 (1981) edited by Carlos Baker

text: That terrible mood of depression of whether it's any good or not is what is known as The Artist's Reward.
author: Ernest Hemingway
source: Letter to F. Scott Fitzgerald (13 September 1929); published in Ernest Hemingway: Selected Letters 1917–1961 (1981) edited by Carlos Baker

text: I know monks masturbate at night That pet cats screw That some girls bite And yet What can I do To set things right?
author: Ernest Hemingway
source: "The Earnest Liberal's Lament" (1924) in The Suppressed Poems (1929)

text: I've been in love (truly) with five women, the Spanish Republic and the 4th Infantry Division.
author: Ernest Hemingway

text: Eschew the monumental. Shun the Epic. All the guys who can paint great big pictures can paint great small ones.
author: Ernest Hemingway
source: Letter (5–6 January 1932); published in Ernest Hemingway: Selected Letters 1917–1961 (1981) edited by Carlos Baker

text: When you have shot one bird flying you have shot all birds flying. They are all different and they fly in different ways but the sensation is the same and the last one is as good as the first.
author: Ernest Hemingway
source: Nick Adams of "Fathers and Sons" in Winner Take Nothing (1932)

text: Our nada who art in nada, nada be thy name thy kingdom nada thy will be nada in nada as it is in nada. Give us this nada our daily nada and nada us our nada as we nada our nadas and nada us not into nada but deliver us from nada; pues nada. Hail nothing full of nothing, nothing is with thee.
author: Ernest Hemingway
source: The old waiter of "A Clean, Well-Lighted Place" in Winner Take Nothing (1932)

text: That is what we are supposed to do when we are at our best — make it all up — but make it up so truly that later it will happen that way.
author: Ernest Hemingway
source: Letter to F. Scott Fitzgerald (28 May 1934); published in Ernest Hemingway: Selected Letters 1917–1961 (1981) edited by Carlos Baker

text: Modern life is often a mechanical oppression, and liquor is the only mechanical relief.
author: Ernest Hemingway
source: Postscript to letter to critic, poet and translator Ivan Kashkin (19 August 1935); published in Ernest Hemingway: Selected Letters 1917–1961 (1981) edited by Carlos Baker

text: I would rather have one honest friend than most of the friends that I have known.
author: Ernest Hemingway
source: Letter to Ivan Kashkin, 19 August 1935, The Letters of Ernest Hemingway, Volume 6, 1934-1936 , Edited by Sandra Spanier, Verna Kale & Miriam B. Mandel, Cambridge University Press, 2024, p. 333

text: I believe in only one thing: liberty. First, I would look after myself and do my work. Then I would care for my family. Then I would help my neighbor. But the state, I care nothing for. I believe in the absolute minimum of government.
author: Ernest Hemingway
source: Letter to Ivan Kashkin, 19 August 1935, The Letters of Ernest Hemingway, Volume 6, 1934-1936 , Edited by Sandra Spanier, Verna Kale & Miriam B. Mandel, Cambridge University Press, 2024, p. 333

text: A writer is like a Gypsy. He owes no allegiance to any government. If he is a good writer, he will never like the government he lives under. His hand should be against it and its hand will always be against him. The minute any bureaucracy passes a certain size, it must be unjust.
author: Ernest Hemingway
source: Letter to Ivan Kashkin, 19 August 1935, The Letters of Ernest Hemingway, Volume 6, 1934-1936 , Edited by Sandra Spanier, Verna Kale & Miriam B. Mandel, Cambridge University Press, 2024, p. 334

text: I've seen a lot of patriots and they all died just like anybody else if it hurt bad enough. Once they were dead, their patriotism was only good for legends; it was bad for their prose and made them write bad poetry. If you are going to be a great patriot, loyal to any existing order of government, you want to be killed early if your life and works won't stink.
author: Ernest Hemingway
source: Letter (12 January 1936); published in Ernest Hemingway: Selected Letters 1917–1961 (1981) edited by Carlos Baker

text: Certainly there is no hunting like the hunting of man and those who have hunted armed men long enough and liked it, never really care for anything else thereafter.
author: Ernest Hemingway

text: Close to the western summit of Kilimanjaro, called by the Masai 'Ngàje Ngài,' the House of God, there is the dried and frozen carcass of a leopard. No one has explained what the leopard was seeking at that altitude.
author: Ernest Hemingway
source: "The Snows of Kilimanjaro," first published in Esquire (August 1936); later published in The Fifth Column and the First Forty-Nine Stories (1938)

text: However you make your living is where your talent lies.
author: Ernest Hemingway
source: "The Snows of Kilimanjaro," first published in Esquire (August 1936); later published in The Fifth Column and the First Forty-Nine Stories (1938)

text: 'The very rich are different from you and me.' 'Yes, they have more money.'
author: Ernest Hemingway
source: "The Snows of Kilimanjaro," first published in Esquire (August 1936); later published in The Fifth Column and the First Forty-Nine Stories (1938). Originally in Esquire "Julian" was named as F. Scott Fitzgerald, who, in "The Rich Boy" (1926) had written: "Let me tell you about the very rich. They are different from you and me. They possess and enjoy early, and it does something to them, makes them soft where we are hard, and cynical where we are trustful, in a way that, unless you were born rich, it is very difficult to understand..." Fitzgerald responded to this in a letter (August 1936) to Hemingway saying: "Riches have never fascinated me, unless combined with the greatest charm or distinction."

text: Anglers have a way of romanticizing their battles with fish and of forgetting that the fish has a hook in his mouth, his gullet, or his belly and that his gameness is really an extreme of panic in which he runs, leaps, and pulls to get away until he dies.
author: Ernest Hemingway
source: Introduction to S. Kip Farrington Jr., Atlantic Game Fishing (1937)

text: There is only one form of government that cannot produce good writers, and that system is Fascism. For Fascism is a lie told by bullies. A writer who will not lie cannot live or work under Fascism. Because Fascism is a lie, it is condemned to literary sterility. And when it is past, it will have no history, except the bloody history of murder.
author: Ernest Hemingway
source: Address, American Writers Congress, New York City (1937). Reprinted in New Masses (June 22, 1937)

text: For our dead are a part of the earth of Spain now and the earth of Spain can never die.
author: Ernest Hemingway
source: "On the American Dead in Spain", New Masses (February 14, 1939)

text: As long as our dead live in the Spanish earth, and they will live as long as the earth lives, no system of tyranny ever will prevail in Spain.
author: Ernest Hemingway
source: "On the American Dead in Spain", New Masses (February 14, 1939)

text: The dead do not need to rise. They are a part of the earth now and the earth can never be conquered. For the earth endureth forever. Those who have entered it honorably, and no man ever entered earth more honorably than those who died in Spain, already have achieved immortality.
author: Ernest Hemingway
source: "On the American Dead in Spain", New Masses (February 14, 1939)

text: There are events which are so great that if a writer has participated in them his obligation is to write truly rather than assume the presumption of altering them with invention.
author: Ernest Hemingway
source: Preface to The Great Crusade (1940) by Gustav Regler

text: I don't like to write like God. It is only because you never do it that the critics think you can't.
author: Ernest Hemingway
source: Letter (26 August 1940); published in Ernest Hemingway: Selected Letters 1917–1961 (1981) edited by Carlos Baker

text: Cowardice, as distinguished from panic, is almost always simply a lack of ability to suspend the functioning of the imagination.
author: Ernest Hemingway

text: Once we have a war there is only one thing to do. It must be won. For defeat brings worse things than any that can ever happen in war.
author: Ernest Hemingway

text: In going where you have to go, and doing what you have to do, and seeing what you have to see, you dull and blunt the instrument you write with. But I would rather have it bent and dulled and know I had to put it on the grindstone again and hammer it into shape, and know that I had something to write about, than to have it bright and shining and nothing to say, or smooth and well oiled in the closet, but unused.
author: Ernest Hemingway
source: Preface to The First Forty-Nine Stories (1944)

text: All my life I've looked at words as though I were seeing them for the first time.
author: Ernest Hemingway
source: Letter (9 April 1945); published in Ernest Hemingway: Selected Letters 1917–1961 (1981) edited by Carlos Baker

text: It wasn't by accident that the Gettysburg address was so short. The laws of prose writing are as immutable as those of flight, of mathematics, of physics.
author: Ernest Hemingway
source: Letter (23 July 1945); published in Ernest Hemingway: Selected Letters 1917–1961 (1981) edited by Carlos Baker

text: It's awfully hard to talk or write about your own stuff because if it is any good you yourself know how good it is — but if you say so yourself you feel like a shit.
author: Ernest Hemingway
source: Letter to Malcolm Cowley (17 October 1945); published in Ernest Hemingway: Selected Letters 1917–1961 (1981) edited by Carlos Baker

text: Do you suffer when you write? I don't at all. I suffer like a bastard when I don't write, or just before, and feel empty and fucked out afterwards. But I never feel as good as while writing.
author: Ernest Hemingway
source: Letter to Malcolm Cowley (14 November 1945); published in Ernest Hemingway: Selected Letters 1917–1961 (1981) edited by Carlos Baker

text: If it's good enough, it will last as long as there are human beings.
author: Ernest Hemingway
source: As quoted in "Portrait of Mr. Papa" by Malcolm Cowley in LIFE magazine (10 January 1949)

text: Literature is just writing as well as you can and finishing what you start.
author: Ernest Hemingway
source: Letter to Arthur Mizener (12 May 1950); published in Ernest Hemingway: Selected Letters 1917–1961 (1981) edited by Carlos Baker

text: I started out very quiet and I beat Mr. Turgenev. Then I trained hard and I beat Mr. de Maupassant. I've fought two draws with Mr. Stendhal, and I think I had an edge in the last one. But nobody's going to get me in any ring with Mr. Tolstoy unless I'm crazy or I keep getting better.
author: Ernest Hemingway
source: Source: quoted in Lillian Ross's profile of Hemingway, which first appeared in the The New Yorker (13 May 1950). The profile was later published as a short book titled Portrait of Hemingway (1961). Variant: I started out very quiet and I beat Turgenev. Then I trained hard and I beat de Maupassant. I've fought two draws with Stendhal, and I think I had an edge in the last one. But nobody's going to get me in any ring with Tolstoy unless I'm crazy or I keep getting better.

text: Wars are Spinach. Life in general is the tough part.
author: Ernest Hemingway

text: Writing and travel broaden your ass if not your mind.
author: Ernest Hemingway
source: Letter (9 July 1950); published in Ernest Hemingway: Selected Letters 1917–1961 (1981) edited by Carlos Baker

text: My health is the main capital I have and I want to administer it intelligently.
author: Ernest Hemingway
source: Letter (21 February 1952); published in Ernest Hemingway: Selected Letters 1917–1961 (1981) edited by Carlos Baker

text: I wouldn't kid Our Lord if he was on the cross. But I would attempt a joke with him if I ran into him chasing the money changers out of the temple.
author: Ernest Hemingway
source: Letter (21 June 1952); published in Ernest Hemingway: Selected Letters 1917–1961 (1981) edited by Carlos Baker

text: There isn't any symbolism. The sea is the sea. The old man is an old man. The boy is a boy and the fish is a fish. What goes beyond is what you see beyond when you know.
author: Ernest Hemingway
source: Letter to Bernard Berenson (13 September 1952); published in Ernest Hemingway: Selected Letters 1917–1961 (1981) edited by Carlos Baker

text: Having books published is very destructive to writing. It is even worse than making love too much. Because when you make love too much at least you get a damned clarity that is like no other light. A very clear and hollow light.
author: Ernest Hemingway
source: Letter to Bernard Berenson (2 October 1952); published in Ernest Hemingway: Selected Letters 1917–1961 (1981) edited by Carlos Baker

text: Fiction is possibly the roughest trade of all in writing. You have the sheet of blank paper, the pencil, and the obligation to invent truer than things can be true. You have to take what is not palpable and make it completely palpable and also have it seem normal and so that it can become a part of experience of the person who reads it.
author: Ernest Hemingway
source: Letter to Bernard Berenson (24 September 1954); published in Ernest Hemingway: Selected Letters 1917–1961 (1981) edited by Carlos Baker

text: You cannot do something someone else has done though you might have done it if they hadn't.
author: Ernest Hemingway
source: Letter (3 July 1956); published in Ernest Hemingway: Selected Letters 1917–1961 (1981) edited by Carlos Baker

text: All poets are crazy. They have to be.
author: Ernest Hemingway
source: As quoted in The New York Post (24 January 1957)

text: It is by riding a bicycle that you learn the contours of a country best, since you have to sweat up the hills and can coast down them. Thus you remember them as they actually are, while in a motorcar only a high hill impresses you, and you have no such accurate remembrance of country you have driven through as you gain by riding a bicycle.
author: Ernest Hemingway
source: White, William, ed (1967). By-Line, Ernest Hemingway: Selected Articles and Dispatches of Four Decades by Ernest Hemingway . New York: Charles Scribner's Sons. p. 364.

text: We are all apprentices in a craft where no one ever becomes a master.
author: Ernest Hemingway

text: We are all bitched from the start and you especially have to be hurt like hell before you can write seriously. But when you get the damned hurt use it — don't cheat with it.
author: Ernest Hemingway
source: Letter to F Scott Fitzgerald, as quoted in Scott Fitzgerald (1962) by Andrew Turnbull (1962) Ch. 14

text: If you have a success, you have it for the wrong reasons. If you become popular it is always because of the worst aspects of your work.
author: Ernest Hemingway
source: As quoted in That Summer in Paris (1963) by Morley Callaghan

text: I learned never to empty the well of my writing, but always to stop when there was still something there in the deep part of the well, and let it refill at night from the springs that fed it.
author: Ernest Hemingway
source: As quoted in Reporting (1964) by Lillian Ross

text: When I have an idea, I turn down the flame, as if it were a little alcohol stove, as low as it will go. Then it explodes and that is my idea.
author: Ernest Hemingway
source: As quoted in Charmed Circle: Gertrude Stein & Co. (1974) by James Mellow

text: You make your own luck. You know what makes a good loser? Practice.
author: Ernest Hemingway
source: Speaking to his son Gregory, as quoted in Papa, a Personal Memoir (1976) Gregory H. Hemingway

text: It's none of their business that you have to learn how to write. Let them think you were born that way.
author: Ernest Hemingway
source: On the loss of a suitcase containing work from his first two years as a writer, as quoted in With Hemingway (1984) by Arnold Samuelson

text: Always do sober what you said you'd do drunk. That will teach you to keep your mouth shut!
author: Ernest Hemingway
source: From a set of "rules for life" sent to publisher Charles Scribner IV; quoted in Scribner's memoir In the Company of Writers (New York: Scribner, 1991), p. 64

text: Listen Jake... don't you ever get the feeling that all your life is going by and you are not taking advantage of it?
author: Ernest Hemingway
source: Robert Cohn to Jake Barnes, in Book 1, Ch. 2

text: You don't want to mix emotions up with a wine like that. You lose the taste.
author: Ernest Hemingway

text: 'How did you go bankrupt?' Bill asked. 'Two ways,' Mike said. 'Gradually and then suddenly.'
author: Ernest Hemingway

text: It's sort of what we have instead of God.
author: Ernest Hemingway
source: Lady Brett Ashley to Jake Barnes, in Book 3, Ch. 19

text: 'Oh, Jake,' Brett said, 'we could have had such a damned good time together.' 'Yes,' I said. 'Isn't it pretty to think so?'
author: Ernest Hemingway
source: Book 3, Ch. 19 (the last lines of the novel)

text: The papers, though written in beautiful language of brotherhood and self-sacrifice, truly stated, with the adjectives removed, that I had been given the medals because I was an American.
author: Ernest Hemingway

text: In the morning there was a big wind blowing and the waves were running high up on the beach and he was awake a long time before he remembered that his heart was broken.
author: Ernest Hemingway

text: I have noticed that doctors who fail in the practice of medicine have a tendency to seek one another's company and aid in consultation. A doctor who cannot take out your appendix properly will recommend you to a doctor who will be unable to remove your tonsils with success.
author: Ernest Hemingway

text: You're my religion. You're all I've got.
author: Ernest Hemingway

text: Life isn't hard to manage when you've nothing to lose.
author: Ernest Hemingway

text: I was always embarrassed by the words sacred, glorious and sacrifice and the expression in vain. I had seen nothing sacred, and the things that were glorious had no glory and the sacrifices were like the stockyards at Chicago if nothing was done with the meat except to bury it.
author: Ernest Hemingway

text: The world breaks everyone and afterward many are strong at the broken places. But those that will not break it kills. It kills the very good and the very gentle and the very brave impartially. If you are none of these you can be sure it will kill you too but there will be no special hurry.
author: Ernest Hemingway

text: No, that is the great fallacy: the wisdom of old men. They do not grow wise. They grow careful.
author: Ernest Hemingway

text: That is all there is to the story. Catherine died and you will die and I will die and that is all I can promise you.
author: Ernest Hemingway
source: One of the alternative endings to the novel, published in A Farewell to Arms: The Special Edition (Penguin Vintage Classics, 2013)

text: About morals, I know only that what is moral is what you feel good after and what is immoral is what you feel bad after.
author: Ernest Hemingway

text: Remember this too: all bad writers are in love with the epic.
author: Ernest Hemingway

text: All our words from loose using have lost their edge.
author: Ernest Hemingway

text: Decadence is a difficult word to use since it has become little more than a term of abuse applied by critics to anything they do not yet understand or which seems to differ from their moral concepts.
author: Ernest Hemingway

text: Bullfighting is the only art in which the artist is in danger of death and in which the degree of brilliance in the performance is left to the fighter's honor.
author: Ernest Hemingway

text: Honor to a Spaniard, no matter how dishonest, is as real a thing as water, wine, or olive oil. There is honor among pickpockets and honor among whores. It is simply that the standards differ.
author: Ernest Hemingway

text: But waiting for a messiah is a long business and you get many fake ones.
author: Ernest Hemingway

text: The great artist uses everything known about his art, instantly absorbing what takes others a lifetime, then goes beyond to make something of his own.
author: Ernest Hemingway

text: There is no remedy for anything in life. Death is a sovereign remedy for all misfortunes.
author: Ernest Hemingway

text: There is no lonelier man in death, except the suicide, than that man who has lived many years with a good wife and then outlived her. If two people love each other there can be no happy end to it.
author: Ernest Hemingway

text: It is an old word, and each one takes it new and wears it out himself. It fills with meaning as a bladder with air, and the meaning goes out of it as quickly. If you have not had it, it does not exist for you.
author: Ernest Hemingway

text: All stories, if continued far enough, end in death, and he is no true-story teller who would keep that from you.
author: Ernest Hemingway

text: It is always a mistake to know an author.
author: Ernest Hemingway

text: Prose is architecture, not interior decoration, and the Baroque is over.
author: Ernest Hemingway

text: If a writer knows enough, he may omit things, and the reader will feel them as strongly as if stated. The dignity of an iceberg's movement is due to only one-eighth being above water. A writer who omits only from ignorance makes hollow places.
author: Ernest Hemingway

text: A serious writer is not to be confused with a solemn writer. A serious writer may be a hawk or a buzzard or even a popinjay, but a solemn writer is always a bloody owl.
author: Ernest Hemingway

text: When writing a novel a writer should create living people; people not characters. A character is a caricature.
author: Ernest Hemingway

text: Some things cannot be learned quickly; time, which is all we have, must be paid heavily for their acquiring. It takes a man's life to know the simplest things, and the little new each man gets from life is very costly, his only heritage.
author: Ernest Hemingway

text: When a man is still in rebellion against death he has pleasure in taking to himself one of the Godlike attributes; that of giving it.
author: Ernest Hemingway

text: The great thing is to last, get your work done, see, hear, learn, and understand; and write when there is something you know, not before, and not too much after.
author: Ernest Hemingway

text: All good books are alike in that they are truer than if they had really happened. After reading one, you feel all that happened to you, and it all belongs to you: the good and bad, ecstasy, remorse, sorrow, people, places, and weather. If you can give that to people, then you are a writer.
author: Ernest Hemingway

text: The hardest thing is to write straight, honest prose on human beings. You must know the subject, then know how to write. Both take a lifetime. Anyone who takes politics as a way out is cheating; all the outs are too easy, and the thing itself is too hard.
author: Ernest Hemingway

text: Personal columnists are jackals, and no jackal has been known to live on grass once he learned about meat — no matter who killed it for him.
author: Ernest Hemingway

text: If a book is good and truly written, you can let the critics yip; their noise will be as pleasant as coyotes on a cold night when you are safe in your own cabin.
author: Ernest Hemingway

text: All the critics who could not make their reputations by discovering you are hoping to make them by predicting your approaching impotence, failure, and drying up of natural juices.
author: Ernest Hemingway
